**CareerPilot AI** - Complete Technical Project Documentation, Architecture, AI/ML Methodology & Jury Preparation Guide

# Executive summary

## What CareerPilot AI is

CareerPilot AI is a web platform that prepares engineering students for campus placement. One student account covers resume analysis, job matching, aptitude and technical assessments, DSA coding practice, AI mock interviews, a placement readiness score, a personalised career plan and mentorship from verified alumni. Placement officers and administrators see the same data as cohort analytics.

**One-sentence technical summary:** it is a three-service system (React, Node.js, Python) in which *deterministic algorithms compute every score* and *language models are used only for language* — asking interview questions, judging free-text answers and phrasing advice — with every model output validated and every final score recomputed in code.

# Problem statement and proposed system

## The problem

A student preparing for placement uses separate tools that do not share information: a resume checker, a coding site, an aptitude site, interview videos and a learning platform. Three problems follow.

- **No single picture.** Nothing tells the student how ready they are overall, or what to fix first.
- **Unexplained scores.** Many resume checkers return a number without saying how it was computed.
- **No institutional view.** A placement officer cannot see which students are at risk until results arrive.

## Existing approach and its limits

| Conventional single-purpose tool | What it typically covers | What it leaves out |
|---|---|---|
| Resume checker | A resume score and keyword hints | Coding, interviews, a plan, institutional view |
| DSA practice site | Problems, judge, submissions | Resume, readiness, career guidance |
| Learning platform | Courses | Personal gap analysis against a target role |
| Job portal | Listings and applications | Preparation and measurement |

This comparison is against a *typical single-purpose* tool. Large commercial platforms offer several of these features together; the claim is about integration and explainability for a campus setting, not about any feature being unique.

## Proposed system

CareerPilot AI puts the preparation steps on one account and connects them through one scoring engine, APIE. Every scored activity (resume, assessment, coding submission, interview answer, alumni feedback) triggers a readiness recomputation, so the dashboard always reflects the latest evidence.

![Figure 2. Student journey](../diagrams/02_user_journey.png)

## Objectives

1. Give each student one explainable readiness score with its components, weights and reasons.
2. Analyse resumes with a transparent rule-based ATS score and job-description comparison.
3. Provide practice for each placement stage: aptitude, coding, technical and HR interviews.
4. Produce a personal career plan from the gap between a student's skills and a target role.
5. Connect students with verified alumni and feed human feedback back into the score.
6. Give placement staff cohort analytics and at-risk identification.
7. Keep AI use safe: validated outputs, deterministic scores, honest labels for prototype models.

# System architecture

## High-level architecture

Three services with one trust boundary. The browser talks only to the Node.js gateway. The gateway is the only caller of the Python AI service, and it authenticates with a shared internal key. Model access and API keys never reach the browser.

```
React (Vite, TypeScript)  --HTTP / WebSocket-->  Node.js + Express gateway  --HTTP + internal key-->  Python FastAPI AI service
   UI, Monaco, voice                              auth, RBAC, MongoDB,                                  agents, NLP, ATS, APIE,
                                                  Socket.IO, PDF, judge                                 RAG, ML, career planner
```

![Figure 1. System architecture (layered)](../diagrams/01_system_architecture.png)

## Why three services instead of one

| Decision | Reason | Alternative considered | Why not |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node.js for the gateway | I/O-heavy work: auth, sockets, database, file streaming | A single Python service | Weaker real-time and WebSocket ergonomics; one service would mix web and ML concerns |
| Python for AI | The NLP/ML libraries (spaCy, scikit-learn, NumPy, PyMuPDF) live there | Running ML in Node | No mature equivalents for spaCy or scikit-learn |
| Shared TypeScript package | Frontend and backend import the same types and enums | Duplicated types | Types drift apart silently |
| Gateway is the only AI caller | One place to enforce auth, rate limits and audit | Browser calls the AI service | Would expose the internal key and bypass access control |

This is a small **service-oriented** design with three services, not a microservices deployment: there is no service discovery, message bus or per-service database.

## Detailed request path

![Figure 3. Request path from browser to model](../diagrams/03_frontend_backend.png)

1. A page component calls a TanStack Query hook, which calls the axios client with the access token.
2. Express runs global middleware: Helmet, CORS, compression, body parsing (2 MB limit), request id, timing, input sanitisation, then the global rate limiter.
3. The route applies `authenticate`, `authorize(role)`, `validate(zodSchema)` and then the controller.
4. The controller calls a service. Services own business rules and Mongoose access.
5. If AI work is needed, `aiClient` posts to FastAPI with the internal key, retries on connection errors and translates failures into typed API errors.
6. In FastAPI, `BaseAgent.run()` validates the input model, runs `handle()`, validates the output model and records latency and provider.

## Layer responsibilities

| Layer | Folder | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Presentation | `frontend/src/pages`, `components`, `layouts` | 38 page components, shared UI kit, route-level code splitting |
| Client state | `frontend/src/store`, TanStack Query | Auth store (Zustand), server-state cache |
| Routes | `backend/src/routes/v1` | 15 route files, 135 endpoints, middleware chains |
| Controllers | `backend/src/controllers` | HTTP in and out; no business rules |
| Services | `backend/src/services` | Business logic, judge, AI client, storage, reports |
| Models | `backend/src/models` | 33 Mongoose models |
| Agents | `ai-service/app/agents` | 11 agents and the orchestrator |
| AI engines | `ai-service/app/services`, `nlp`, `rag`, `ml`, `career` | Deterministic engines and model wrappers |
| Shared | `shared/src` | Types, enums, constants used by both TypeScript apps |
| Seed data | `database/seeds` | Demo companies, questions, DSA problems and reference solutions |

## Real-time and background behaviour

- **Socket.IO** pushes notifications and `readiness:updated`, and carries WebRTC signalling for the alumni interview room. [IMPLEMENTED]
- **There is no job queue or worker process.** The DSA judge runs inside the request, bounded by an in-process semaphore (`CODE_RUNNER_MAX_CONCURRENT`, default 2; up to 25 requests wait, more are refused). A queue with separate judge workers is [PLANNED].
- **There is no external cache** such as Redis. Caching is limited to an in-memory configuration cache, a 20-second cache of the Docker availability check, and the browser-side TanStack Query cache.

> **Check before the demo.** The repository's local settings use `AI_PROVIDER=mock`, `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=hash` and `VECTOR_DB_PROVIDER=numpy`. With the mock provider, interview questions and written feedback come from an offline rule-based generator, **not a language model**. Scores are unaffected because they are computed in code. If a judge asks "which LLM is answering right now?", the truthful answer depends on that setting.

# Database architecture

**Technology:** MongoDB 7 through Mongoose 8. There are **33 models** and about 186 index declarations. MongoDB has no foreign keys; relationships are `ObjectId` references that Mongoose can populate, and integrity is enforced in the service layer.

![Figure 4. Main collections and how they relate](../diagrams/04_database.png)

## Collections by purpose

| Group | Models |
|---|---|
| Identity and audit | User, RefreshToken, AuditLog, Notification |
| Profiles | StudentProfile, AlumniProfile, PlacementOfficer |
| Resume | Resume, ResumeAnalysis |
| Jobs | Company, JobRole, JobDescription, Skill |
| Assessment | Assessment, AssessmentQuestion, AssessmentAttempt, MonitoringEvent |
| Coding | CodingProblem, CodingSubmission |
| Interview | InterviewSession, InterviewQuestion, InterviewResponse, InterviewEvaluation |
| Readiness | PlacementReadiness, SkillGap, Recommendation |
| Career | CareerPlan |
| Mentorship | MentorshipRequest, MentorshipSession, AlumniFeedback |
| AI and configuration | AIInteraction, RAGDocument, SystemConfiguration |

There is no separate "Admin" model: an administrator is a `User` with role `ADMIN`. There is no separate "Resource" collection: learning resources are a JSON catalogue inside the AI service.

## Relationships

| Relationship | Type | How it is stored |
|---|---|---|
| User — StudentProfile / AlumniProfile / PlacementOfficer | One-to-one | Profile holds `userId` (unique) |
| StudentProfile — Resume | One-to-many | Resume holds `studentId`; one is marked `isPrimary` |
| Resume — ResumeAnalysis | One-to-many | Each re-analysis adds a record |
| StudentProfile — PlacementReadiness | One-to-many | Append-only snapshots; the newest is current |
| StudentProfile — CodingSubmission — CodingProblem | Many-to-many through a join document | Submission holds `studentId` and `problemId` |
| Assessment — AssessmentQuestion | One-to-many | Question holds `assessmentId` |
| StudentProfile — AssessmentAttempt — Assessment | Many-to-many through a join document | Attempt holds both ids |
| InterviewSession — Question — Response — Evaluation | One-to-many chain | Each child holds its parent id |
| Company — JobRole — JobDescription | One-to-many | Child holds parent id |
| StudentProfile — target companies and roles | Many-to-many | Arrays of ids on the profile |
| MentorshipRequest — MentorshipSession — AlumniFeedback | One-to-one, then one-to-many | Child holds parent id |

## Schemas worth knowing

**User.** `email` (unique), `passwordHash`, `fullName`, `role`, `status`, `emailVerified`. The password is never stored in plain text.

**ResumeAnalysis.** `atsScore`, `parsed`, `breakdown` (the nine criteria), `matchedKeywords`, `missingKeywords`, `strengths`, `weaknesses`, recommendations, `targetJobDescriptionId`, `jobDescriptionSource` (CATALOGUE or CUSTOM), `jobMatchScore`, `engineVersion`, `provenance`.

**PlacementReadiness.** `score`, `band`, `components` (key, raw, normalised, weight, weighted, evidence count, stale flag), `modifiers`, `weightsSnapshot`, ML prediction, `trigger`, `computedAt`. Storing the weights with each snapshot keeps old scores interpretable after weights change.

**CodingProblem.** `title`, `slug` (unique), `difficulty`, `tags`, `description`, `examples`, `constraints`, `functionName`, `signature`, `compareMode`, `starterCode`, `supportedLanguages`, `testCases`, `hiddenTestCases`, `referenceSolutions`, `timeLimitMs` (default 2000), `memoryLimitMb` (default 128). `hiddenTestCases` and `referenceSolutions` are declared `select: false`, so no query returns them unless it asks for them by name.

**CodingSubmission.** `problemId`, `studentId`, `language`, `code`, `status` (the verdict), `passedCount`, `totalCount`, `runtimeMs`, `memoryKb`, `execution`, `score`, `aiReview`.

**CareerPlan.** Target role, inputs, the generated plan, resources, `resourcesBySkill`, schedule, readiness summary, progress, and which engine produced it.

## Why MongoDB

The data is document-shaped and evolves: a resume analysis, a readiness snapshot and a career plan are nested structures whose fields changed during development. A relational schema would need many join tables and migrations. The cost is weaker referential integrity, which is handled in services, and no multi-document transactions are relied on.

# Security architecture

![Figure 17. Security controls by layer](../diagrams/17_security.png)

| Concern | Control | Where | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Passwords | bcrypt hash with salt, 12 rounds | `User` model | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Sessions | JWT access token (15 min) and refresh token (7 days) | auth service | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Stolen refresh token | Rotation with family revocation: reuse of an old token revokes the whole family | auth service | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Refresh token storage | Signed `httpOnly` cookie | auth controller | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Authorisation | `authorize(role)` middleware; ownership checks in controllers | routes | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Input validation | Zod schemas on body, query and params | `validators/` | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| NoSQL injection | `sanitizeInput` strips operator keys; validated types | middleware | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| XSS | React escapes output; Helmet headers; downloads sent as attachments with `nosniff` | frontend, backend | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| CSRF | Access token travels in a header, not a cookie; CORS allow-list | backend | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Rate limiting | Global, auth, AI, upload and code-run limiters | middleware | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| File upload | Extension + MIME type + magic bytes + 5 MB limit + SHA-256 duplicate check | upload middleware, storage | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Secrets | Environment variables; `.env` not committed; `.env.example` has no real values | config | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Service boundary | AI service requires an internal key and is not exposed publicly | ai-service | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Audit | Sensitive actions written to `AuditLog` | audit service | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Error handling | Central handler returns coded errors; stack traces are not sent to clients | middleware | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Code execution | Isolated container, never on the host | judge | [PARTIALLY IMPLEMENTED] (not run with Docker yet) |

## AI-specific security

| Risk | What the project does | What it does not do |
|---|---|---|
| Hallucinated scores | The model returns dimension scores; the overall is recomputed in code | — |
| Hallucinated facts | Strict Pydantic schemas (`extra="forbid"`); ATS grounding guard moves an unmatched "matched skill" to missing | — |
| Hallucinated links | The career model may output resource IDs only; unknown IDs are dropped | — |
| Unsupported answers | RAG returns a fixed "no verified information" answer below the relevance threshold, without calling the LLM | — |
| Prompt injection | Structural limits: the model cannot call tools, cannot set a final score, and its output must match a schema | There is **no dedicated prompt-injection classifier or filter** |
| Server-side request forgery | The resource verifier allows only HTTPS on the provider's domain, refuses private addresses, re-checks redirects | — |
| Bias from voice | Whether an answer was spoken or typed is not sent to the evaluator | — |

> **If asked "how do you stop prompt injection?"** Do not claim a filter. Say: "A resume or answer could contain instructions, so the design limits what the model can do with them. It has no tools, it cannot decide a score because the score is recomputed from fixed weights, and anything outside the schema is rejected. A dedicated injection detector is future work."

# Functional modules

Each module below follows the same template so you can answer "what goes in, what happens, what comes out" for any of them. Complexity uses *n* for the size of the input named in each block.

## Authentication and role-based access

- **Problem:** only the right person may see or change a record.
- **Input:** email and password; later an access token on each request.
- **Processing:** the password is compared with its bcrypt hash. On success the server issues a 15-minute JWT access token and a 7-day refresh token stored as a signed `httpOnly` cookie. Each refresh issues a new refresh token; presenting an old one revokes the whole token family.
- **Algorithm:** bcrypt (12 rounds); HMAC-signed JWT; refresh-token rotation with family revocation.
- **Technology:** Express middleware `authenticate`, `authorize(role)`, `requireStudentProfile`.
- **Database:** `User`, `RefreshToken`, `AuditLog`.
- **AI:** none.
- **Output:** tokens and the user's profile; 401 or 403 otherwise.
- **Time complexity:** O(1) per request plus the fixed bcrypt cost at login. **Space:** O(1).
- **Advantages:** stateless access checks; a stolen refresh token is detected on reuse.
- **Limitations:** no multi-factor authentication.
- **Status:** [IMPLEMENTED]

## Resume intelligence and ATS scoring

This is the module the jury will probe most. The full pipeline is deterministic.

![Figure 5. Resume / ATS pipeline](../diagrams/05_ats_pipeline.png)

- **Problem:** a student does not know why a resume scores low or what to change.
- **Input:** a PDF, DOCX or TXT file up to 5 MB; optionally a job description (predefined, pasted, or uploaded as a file).
- **Processing:**
  1. **Ingestion.** Extension, MIME type and magic bytes are checked; a SHA-256 checksum short-circuits duplicate uploads.
  2. **Text extraction.** PyMuPDF for PDF, python-docx for DOCX. Fewer than 120 characters is rejected (usually a scanned image; there is no OCR).
  3. **Section detection.** A line of at most 45 characters matching a known heading starts a section.
  4. **Field extraction.** Regular expressions for email, phone, links, CGPA, dates; spaCy NER for the name.
  5. **Skill extraction.** A taxonomy of 107 canonical skills with 181 aliases, matched with custom word boundaries so `C++` and `C#` work and "Java" is not found inside "JavaScript".
  6. **Scoring.** Nine criteria, each a capped formula.
  7. **JD comparison.** JD keywords are canonicalised; `coverage = matched / (matched + missing) × 100`.
  8. **Recommendations.** Generated from the criteria that lost points.
- **Algorithm:** rule-based NLP (regex, dictionary matching, NER) and weighted multi-criteria scoring.
- **Technology:** FastAPI, spaCy, PyMuPDF, python-docx.
- **Database:** `Resume` (file metadata), `ResumeAnalysis` (result). The file itself is in local or S3 storage.
- **AI:** deterministic by default. The optional fine-tuned model is described in the AI chapter and is off.
- **Output:** ATS score out of 100, per-criterion breakdown, extracted profile, matched and missing keywords, strengths, weaknesses, recommendations.
- **Time complexity:** O(n · t) for text length *n* and *t* taxonomy patterns (288 terms). **Space:** O(n).
- **Advantages:** explainable, repeatable, needs no GPU or training data, cannot invent a skill.
- **Limitations:** finds only skills in the taxonomy; no OCR; it approximates ATS behaviour and is not any employer's real system.
- **Status:** [IMPLEMENTED]

### The nine ATS criteria

| Criterion | Points | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Skills coverage | 20 | min(8, skills × 0.55) + min(4, languages × 1.4) + min(4, frameworks × 1.2) + min(4, CS fundamentals × 1.4) |
| Section structure | 15 | (required sections found ÷ required) × 9 + min(6, optional sections × 1.5) |
| Experience evidence | 15 | min(7, projects × 2.2) + min(5, internships × 2.5) + min(3, jobs × 3) |
| Contact information | 10 | name 3 + email 3 + phone 2 + LinkedIn/GitHub 2 |
| Education details | 10 | education 4 + CGPA 3 + institution 1.5 + graduation year 1.5 |
| Quantified impact | 10 | min(10, quantified phrases × 1.8) |
| Formatting hygiene | 10 | starts at 10, with deductions for few bullets, very long lines, table layout, unusual symbols |
| Action verbs | 5 | min(5, distinct verbs × 0.45) − min(2, weak phrases × 0.7) |
| Length | 5 | 200–700 words scores 5; shorter or longer scores less |

Each `min(...)` is a cap. It gives diminishing returns, so listing forty skills cannot outscore a balanced resume. Projects weigh more than jobs because the users are freshers.

### Which parts are deterministic and which use AI

| Step | Deterministic | Uses a model |
|---|---|---|
| Text extraction, sections, fields | Yes | spaCy NER for the name only (a pre-trained statistical model) |
| Skill extraction | Yes (dictionary) | No |
| ATS score | Yes | No |
| Matched / missing keywords | Yes | No, even when the fine-tuned model is enabled |
| Strengths, weaknesses, advice | Yes (templates) | Optional fine-tuned model, currently off |

## Job matching

- **Problem:** which jobs suit this profile, and what is missing for a given job.
- **Input:** the student's skills, CGPA and backlogs; a job description.
- **Processing and algorithm:**

```
match = 0.55 × required-skill coverage
      + 0.20 × preferred-skill coverage
      + 0.15 × semantic similarity (profile text vs JD text)
      + 0.10 × eligibility fit (CGPA, backlogs)
```

- Coverage is computed on canonical skills. Similarity is the cosine of two embedding vectors. Failing a stated CGPA or backlog limit sets `eligible = false` whatever the score.
- **Database:** `JobDescription`, `Company`, `JobRole`, `StudentProfile`.
- **AI:** embeddings only; no generative model.
- **Output:** match score, missing skills, eligibility, a preparation plan.
- **Time complexity:** O(s + d) for *s* skills and embedding dimension *d* = 384. **Space:** O(d).
- **Limitations:** the default embedding is lexical, not semantic.
- **Status:** [IMPLEMENTED]

## Assessment engine

- **Problem:** fair, recoverable timed tests.
- **Processing:** the deadline is stored on the server and the browser timer is only a display. Answers autosave and survive a refresh. Grading happens on the server; correct answers never reach the browser. Integrity signals such as tab switches produce a LOW, MEDIUM or HIGH indicator for a human to review.
- **Algorithm:** server-authoritative timing; rule-based grading; threshold-based integrity level.
- **Database:** `Assessment`, `AssessmentQuestion`, `AssessmentAttempt`, `MonitoringEvent`.
- **AI:** none.
- **Output:** score, topic breakdown, and the integrity log shown openly to the student.
- **Time complexity:** O(q) for *q* questions.
- **Limitations:** a signal never fails a student automatically, by design.
- **Status:** [IMPLEMENTED]

## DSA practice and the online judge

![Figure 11. DSA judge: from Submit to verdict](../diagrams/11_dsa_judge.png)

- **Problem:** practise coding questions and get a trustworthy verdict.
- **Input:** a language (Python, C++, Java or JavaScript) and the body of one function.
- **Processing:**
  1. **Problem management.** 28 problems across 16 topic tags and three difficulties, loaded from `database/seeds/dsaProblems.ts` by `npm run seed:dsa`. Each has a typed signature, public tests and hidden tests.
  2. **Code generation.** From the signature the backend generates the starter code and a harness per language. The harness reads arguments from standard input, calls the function and writes the returned value as JSON to a result file. Standard output stays free for the student's own prints.
  3. **Execution.** One throw-away container per submission compiles once, then runs each test. The host streams test inputs one at a time.
  4. **Judging.** The host compares each returned value with the expected value and classifies the test.
  5. **Storage.** Submit stores the verdict, counts, runtime and memory. Run stores nothing.
- **Algorithm:** code generation from a typed signature; structural JSON comparison; verdict classification.
- **Technology:** Node.js `child_process.spawn` of the Docker CLI with a fixed argument list; Monaco editor in the browser.
- **Database:** `CodingProblem`, `CodingSubmission`.
- **AI:** none in the verdict. After the verdict is final, an advisory "Static Code Analysis" is requested.
- **Output:** verdict, passed count, runtime, memory, per-test detail for public tests only.
- **Time complexity:** O(T · L) wall time for *T* tests and time limit *L*; the comparator is O(size of the answer). **Space:** bounded by the memory limit.
- **Status:** judge logic [IMPLEMENTED]; container isolation [PARTIALLY IMPLEMENTED] — written and unit-tested, not yet executed on a machine with Docker.

### What exists and what does not

| Item in a typical online judge | In this project |
|---|---|
| Problem list with search, difficulty and tag filters | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Monaco editor, language switch, per-language starter code | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Languages | Python (CPython 3), C++17 (g++), Java (OpenJDK), JavaScript (Node.js). **C is not supported.** |
| Run on public tests; Submit on public + hidden tests | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Submission history and solved progress | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| Reference solutions and test validation | [IMPLEMENTED] — stored server-side; the test suite requires every one to be Accepted |
| Admin screen to create or publish problems | [PLANNED] — problems come from the seed file |
| Queue and separate judge workers | [PLANNED] — an in-process concurrency limiter is used |
| Custom test input from the editor | [PLANNED] |

### Verdicts

| Verdict | When | Status |
|---|---|---|
| ACCEPTED | Every test ran and matched | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| WRONG_ANSWER | Returned value differs from expected | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| COMPILATION_ERROR | Compile or syntax check failed; no test runs | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| RUNTIME_ERROR | Non-zero exit, or no value returned | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| TIME_LIMIT_EXCEEDED | Stopped at the limit | [IMPLEMENTED] |
| MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED | Killed for memory, or an out-of-memory error | Classification [IMPLEMENTED]; real enforcement needs the container |
| INTERNAL_ERROR | The sandbox could not run the code | [IMPLEMENTED] — reported as "not executed", never guessed |
| OUTPUT_LIMIT_EXCEEDED | — | Not a separate verdict. Output is truncated at 64 KB; an oversized report stream is treated as a sandbox failure |

The verdict of a submission is the verdict of its **first failing test**. Score = passed ÷ total × 100.

### Why user code must not run on the backend

Submitted code is untrusted. On the API host it could read environment secrets, open the database, read other students' files, or exhaust the machine. Running it in the Node process (`eval`, `vm`) is not a security boundary. The project therefore has exactly one way to run student code: inside a container.

![Figure 12. Sandbox isolation applied to every container](../diagrams/12_docker_sandbox.png)

| Limit | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Network | `--network none` |
| Filesystem | `--read-only`, tmpfs for `/work` and `/tmp`, no volumes |
| Identity | `--user 65534:65534`, `--cap-drop ALL`, `no-new-privileges` |
| Memory | `--memory` and `--memory-swap`; plus per language: Java `-Xmx`, Node `--max-old-space-size`, C++ address-space limit |
| CPU and processes | `--cpus`, `--pids-limit` (stops fork bombs) |
| Time | `timeout` inside the container and a host-side deadline; default 2 s, scaled ×1 C++, ×2 Java, ×2 JavaScript, ×3 Python |
| Secrets | no `-e` flags, so no host environment variable enters |
| Cleanup | `--rm` plus an explicit `docker rm -f` |

### Hidden-test security

- Expected outputs **never enter the container**; comparison happens on the host.
- Inputs are streamed one test at a time, public tests first, so hidden inputs are not present while public tests run.
- `hiddenTestCases` is excluded from every database query unless the judge asks for it by name.
- In a response, a hidden test appears only as passed/failed, its status and its timing. An API test asserts that hidden inputs never appear in any response or stored record.

If hidden tests were exposed, a student could hard-code the expected answers and "pass" without solving the problem.

## AI mock interview

- **Problem:** practise answering aloud or in text and get specific feedback.
- **Input:** mode (technical, HR, behavioural), difficulty, number of questions, then each answer (typed, or spoken and transcribed into an editable transcript).
- **Processing:** generate a question → the student answers → the evaluator scores five dimensions → the overall score is recomputed in code → difficulty adapts → next question.
- **Algorithm:**
  - *Difficulty controller:* look at the last three answer scores; mean ≥ 78 steps up, ≤ 42 steps down, otherwise hold. Nothing changes until two answers exist.
  - *Score:* weighted sum of relevance, correctness, completeness, communication and structure, with weights that depend on the mode (technical gives correctness 0.35; behavioural gives structure 0.25).
  - *Delivery signals:* word count, filler-word rate, `clarity = 100 − 600 × fillerRate − 6 × hedgeCount`. Computed from the transcript text only.
- **Technology:** LLM provider interface (or the mock provider), Web Speech API for speech-to-text and text-to-speech, optional server Whisper fallback.
- **Database:** `InterviewSession`, `InterviewQuestion`, `InterviewResponse`, `InterviewEvaluation`.
- **AI:** an LLM writes questions and scores the five dimensions. It does not compute the overall score.
- **Output:** per-answer scores, strengths, improvements, a session report.
- **Limitations:** with `AI_PROVIDER=mock` the questions and feedback come from an offline generator, not a language model.
- **Status:** [IMPLEMENTED]

## APIE — Placement Readiness Score

![Figure 14. What triggers a readiness update](../diagrams/14_student_workflow.png)

- **Problem:** turn scattered results into one explainable number and a priority list.
- **Input:** every scored activity for the student.
- **Processing and algorithm:**
  1. **Recency weighting.** Per component, `value = Σ(score_i × 1/(i+1)) / Σ 1/(i+1)`, newest first. The newest result has weight 1, then ½, then ⅓.
  2. **Weighted base.** Coding 0.25, technical interview 0.20, communication 0.15, resume/ATS 0.10, HR interview 0.10, aptitude 0.10, academic 0.10.
  3. **Bounded modifiers.** Projects up to +3, certifications up to +2, internships up to +3, alumni feedback −4 to +4.
  4. **Bands.** Below 40 At Risk; 40–60 Needs Improvement; 60–80 Placement Ready; 80 and above Highly Ready.
- **Database:** `PlacementReadiness` (append-only), `SkillGap`, `Recommendation`.
- **AI:** none in the score. A Random Forest gives a second opinion beside it.
- **Output:** score, band, component breakdown, strengths, weaknesses, skill gaps, recommendations, trend.
- **Time complexity:** O(e) for *e* evidence items.
- **Advantages:** weighted, recency-aware and evidence-aware; missing evidence is shown as "no evidence", never as a silent zero.
- **Limitations:** the weights are a design choice and are **not validated against real placement outcomes**. Every screen labels it a prototype scoring model.
- **Status:** [IMPLEMENTED]

## Career Plan

![Figure 6. Career Plan pipeline](../diagrams/06_career_pipeline.png)

- **Problem:** "what should I learn, in what order, in the time I have, and from where?"
- **Input:** current skills with levels, target role (one of 20), hours per day, days per week, optional deadline, optional ATS result, optional progress.
- **Processing:**
  1. **Skill normalisation** against 122 skills and 214 aliases.
  2. **Prerequisite inference.** Knowing React at intermediate level is treated as evidence of at least beginner JavaScript.
  3. **Gap analysis.** For each role requirement, gap = required level above current level; missing prerequisites of gap skills are added.
  4. **Priority score.** `importance × 10 + 8 if core + 6 per skill it unblocks (cap 24) + 12 if the ATS analysis listed it as missing + 4 per level to climb`. HIGH at 62 or more, MEDIUM at 40 or more, otherwise LOW.
  5. **Planning.** Phases follow the prerequisite graph (123 edges, verified acyclic, depth 6), so a skill is never scheduled before what it depends on.
  6. **Time budget.** 75% learning, 15% projects, 10% revision and interview preparation. If a deadline does not fit, low-priority gaps are deferred first; a skill is never deferred while a kept skill depends on it; if it still does not fit, the plan says the deadline is not achievable.
  7. **Resources.** Candidates are chosen by ID from the verified catalogue.
- **Algorithm:** graph-based prerequisite ordering (topological order), additive priority scoring, feasibility-constrained scheduling.
- **Technology:** Python, JSON knowledge files under `ai-service/app/career/data`.
- **Database:** `CareerPlan`.
- **AI:** the rule-based planner produces every plan. The fine-tuned model is optional and off.
- **Output:** readiness summary, skill gaps with reasons, phased plan, weekly and daily schedule, projects, interview topics, resources per skill.
- **Time complexity:** O(V + E) for the graph (122 + 123) plus O(g log g) to sort *g* gaps.
- **Limitations:** the role knowledge (levels, hours, prerequisites) was written by one author and is not validated; 81% of role-to-skill links are corroborated by O*NET, ESCO or job postings, which supports the mapping only.
- **Status:** [IMPLEMENTED] with the planner; model path [PARTIALLY IMPLEMENTED].

## Learning-resource recommendation and YouTube integration

![Figure 9. Resource recommendation and verification](../diagrams/09_resource_pipeline.png)

- **Problem:** recommend material that exists and matches the skill and level.
- **Input:** a skill, a stage (beginner, intermediate, advanced), an optional preference.
- **Processing:** look up the catalogue by skill; score each resource `3.0 (covers the skill) + 2.0 if the difficulty matches the stage + 1.5 if verified (0.5 if only reachable) + quality weight (0 to 1) + 0.5 if the type matches the learner's preference + 0.3 if the language matches`; ties break on the resource ID so the order is reproducible. Unreachable resources are excluded.
- **The catalogue:** 270 resources — 65 documentation pages, 13 free courses, 8 practice platforms, 4 books and 180 YouTube videos. 239 verified, 29 reachable, 2 unreachable and excluded. 112 of 122 skills have at least one usable resource.
- **Verification:** each non-video URL was fetched over HTTPS. The verifier refuses anything but HTTPS on the provider's own domain, refuses hosts resolving to private or loopback addresses, follows at most three redirects and caps the bytes read. Videos were checked through the YouTube Data API as public and embeddable.
- **AI:** none. `quality_score` is an editorial weight by resource type, not a user rating.
- **Status:** [IMPLEMENTED]

![Figure 10. YouTube integration](../diagrams/10_youtube_integration.png)

### Why the language model must not memorise links

| Layer | Job | Why it is separate |
|---|---|---|
| Language model | Reasoning, personalisation, wording | A model's knowledge is frozen at training time |
| Retrieval layer | Current resources | Videos and courses are removed, renamed or replaced |
| Verification layer | Does the link work | A model cannot check a URL; it can only produce one that looks right |
| Ranking layer | Which resource fits | Ranking rules can change without retraining |

A model asked to recall a URL will produce a plausible string that may never have existed. In this project the model is given resource **IDs** in the prompt and may only choose among them. An ID that is not in the catalogue is dropped and counted as a hallucination. A new resource therefore works without retraining.

## RAG knowledge base

- **Problem:** answer placement questions from stored documents without inventing facts.
- **Processing:** documents are split into chunks of 900 characters with 150 overlap on paragraph and sentence boundaries, embedded, and stored. A question is embedded, the top 5 chunks are retrieved by cosine similarity, and chunks below the threshold (0.18 for the lexical embedder, 0.25 for semantic ones) are discarded. **If nothing survives, the LLM is not called** and a fixed "no verified information" answer is returned.
- **Database:** `RAGDocument`; vectors in the NumPy store by default.
- **Time complexity:** O(N · d) per query (exact search over *N* chunks of dimension *d*).
- **Limitations:** exact brute-force search suits a small corpus only.
- **Status:** [IMPLEMENTED]; available through the admin console.

## Alumni mentorship

- **Processing:** mentors are ranked by `0.35 company + 0.20 role + 0.20 skills + 0.15 gap coverage + 0.05 rating + 0.05 availability`. A request leads to a scheduled session in a WebRTC room (signalling over Socket.IO). Structured feedback becomes a bounded ±4 modifier in APIE.
- **Database:** `AlumniProfile`, `MentorshipRequest`, `MentorshipSession`, `AlumniFeedback`.
- **Limitations:** WebRTC through restrictive networks needs a TURN server, which is configuration only.
- **Status:** [IMPLEMENTED]

## Analytics, reports and administration

![Figure 13. Administrator and placement-officer workflow](../diagrams/13_admin_workflow.png)

- **Placement officer:** cohort readiness, band distribution, common skill gaps, at-risk students, department comparison, a pseudonymised research export.
- **Administrator:** users and roles, companies and jobs, alumni verification, knowledge base, APIE weights (validated to sum to 1.0), AI usage per agent, audit log, flagged assessment attempts.
- **Reports:** ten PDF report types generated with PDFKit.
- **Algorithm:** MongoDB aggregation pipelines.
- **Status:** [IMPLEMENTED]

# AI architecture

## The design rule

Every AI feature separates seven things. Being able to name them is the strongest answer you can give about the AI design.

| Part | In CareerPilot |
|---|---|
| MODEL | An LLM provider (or the mock), a Random Forest, optional Qwen3 adapters |
| DATA | Resumes, job descriptions, curated role knowledge, synthetic learner profiles |
| TRAINING | Offline, in Colab notebooks; never inside the application |
| INFERENCE | One call through the provider interface, with a timeout |
| RETRIEVAL | The RAG vector store and the resource catalogue |
| VERIFICATION | Pydantic schemas, grounding checks, resource-ID resolution, URL checks |
| DETERMINISTIC LOGIC | ATS score, APIE, job match, judge verdicts, the planner, all final arithmetic |

![Figure 15. AI architecture: what is deterministic and what is a model](../diagrams/15_ai_architecture.png)

## Agents and orchestration

An agent is a class with one responsibility, a typed input schema, a typed output schema and a `handle()` method. `BaseAgent.run()` wraps every agent with the same four steps: validate input, run, validate output, record latency and provider.

| Agent | Responsibility | Uses an LLM |
|---|---|---|
| Resume Intelligence | Parse a resume, compute the ATS score, match JD keywords | Only to phrase advice, and only if the fine-tuned model is enabled |
| Job Matching | Score a student against a job | No |
| Coding Assessment | Static review of submitted code (advisory) | Yes |
| Technical / HR / Behavioural Interview | Generate the next question | Yes |
| Interview Evaluation | Score an answer on five dimensions | Yes; overall recomputed in code |
| Placement Readiness | Run APIE | No |
| Alumni Mentorship, Feedback Ingest | Match mentors; convert human feedback to signals | No |
| Analytics | Cohort statistics | No |

There are **11 registered agents** and two fixed workflows: `RESUME_TO_MATCH` and `INTERVIEW_TURN`.

**Agents never call each other.** Composition happens only in the orchestrator, so the call graph is acyclic and every multi-step flow is a named, auditable operation.

> **If asked "is this really agentic AI?"** It is a multi-agent architecture with orchestrated, deterministic workflows. The agents are specialised and adaptive, but they do not plan autonomously or call tools in a loop. That was chosen for auditability in an assessment system.

## The LLM layer

One interface (`complete_json`) with four providers selected by `AI_PROVIDER`: `openai` (any OpenAI-compatible endpoint), `azure`, `ollama` and `mock`. This is the Strategy pattern.

Three controls apply wherever a model is called:

1. **Structured output.** Prompts demand JSON matching a schema; the response is parsed and validated.
2. **Low temperature** (0.15–0.2 for evaluation) so the same answer gets a consistent score.
3. **Score recomputation.** The model returns dimension scores; the overall is recomputed from fixed weights.

**The mock provider is not a language model.** It assembles schema-valid responses with rules over the real input so the platform runs offline. Every mock response is tagged `provider: "mock"`.

# Algorithms used in CareerPilot

Only algorithms present in the source are listed. TF-IDF and a learned neural ranker are **not** used anywhere; do not claim them.

## Summary table

| # | Algorithm | Used for | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dictionary matching with custom word boundaries | Skill extraction | O(n · t) |
| 2 | Pattern-based section detection | Resume structure | O(lines) |
| 3 | Named-entity recognition (spaCy) | Candidate name | Linear in text |
| 4 | Capped weighted multi-criteria scoring | ATS score, APIE, job match, mentor match | O(k) criteria |
| 5 | Feature hashing with sub-linear term frequency | Default text embedding | O(n) |
| 6 | Cosine similarity | Job match, RAG | O(d) |
| 7 | Exact vector search | RAG retrieval | O(N · d) |
| 8 | Overlapping boundary-aware chunking | RAG ingestion | O(n) |
| 9 | Relevance-threshold gating | Hallucination control in RAG | O(k) |
| 10 | Harmonic recency weighting | APIE evidence | O(e) |
| 11 | Random Forest (and Gradient Boosting) | Readiness band second opinion | Train O(trees · n log n) |
| 12 | Threshold controller | Interview difficulty | O(1) |
| 13 | Topological ordering of a prerequisite graph | Career plan phases | O(V + E) |
| 14 | Additive priority scoring | Skill-gap priority | O(g) |
| 15 | Feasibility-constrained scheduling with deferral | Study plan | O(g log g) |
| 16 | Deterministic resource ranking | Resource recommendation | O(r log r) |
| 17 | Item-based collaborative filtering | Skill recommender (not live) | O(s · V) per query |
| 18 | MinHash + LSH near-duplicate clustering | ATS dataset splitting | Near-linear |
| 19 | Code generation from a typed signature | DSA harness and starter code | O(parameters) |
| 20 | Structural JSON comparison with tolerance | Judge comparator | O(answer size) |
| 21 | Verdict classification | Judge | O(1) per test |
| 22 | bcrypt, HMAC-signed JWT, token rotation | Security | Fixed cost |
| 23 | QLoRA | Fine-tuning both models | See training chapter |

## Skill extraction — dictionary matching

- **Input:** resume or JD text. **Output:** canonical skill names.
- **How it works:** each of 107 skills and 181 aliases is compiled to a regular expression with the boundary `(?<![a-zA-Z0-9+#])term(?![a-zA-Z0-9+#])`. Separators inside a term are flexible, so `node.js`, `node js` and `nodejs` all match. Aliases map to one canonical name.
- **Why selected:** deterministic, explainable, needs no training data, cannot invent a skill.
- **Alternative:** a neural NER model for skills. **Why not:** needs labelled data, can hallucinate, and is harder to explain to a student.
- **Limitation:** finds only skills in the taxonomy.

## Feature hashing embedding

- **Input:** text. **Output:** a 384-dimensional unit vector.
- **Steps:** tokenise and count; weight each token `(1 + ln(count)) × sign`; add it to bucket `MD5(token) mod 384`; for tokens longer than five characters add character trigrams at weight 0.25; L2-normalise.
- **Why selected:** needs no download, no network and no GPU.
- **Alternative:** `sentence-transformers` (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) or OpenAI embeddings, selectable with `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER`. **Why not default:** they need a model download or an API key.
- **Be precise:** this is a *lexical* embedding. It captures shared words, not meaning.

## Cosine similarity and vector search

`cos(a, b) = (a · b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖)`. All vectors are L2-normalised, so cosine similarity equals the dot product and a search is one matrix–vector multiplication. The NumPy store and FAISS `IndexFlatIP` are both **exact** search. Approximate indexes (HNSW, IVF) are not used because the corpus is small.

## Harmonic recency weighting

```
value = Σ (score_i × 1/(i+1)) / Σ 1/(i+1)        i = 0 for the newest result
```

Improvement shows quickly, but one bad day does not erase a track record. **Alternative:** a plain mean (ignores recency) or latest-only (too noisy).

## Random Forest

- **Task:** classify a student into one of four readiness bands from 14 features (7 component scores, project count, certification count, internship months, alumni feedback score, open skill gaps, assessments taken, interviews taken).
- **Settings:** 300 trees, max depth 12, minimum 4 samples per leaf, balanced class weights, `StandardScaler → classifier`, 80/20 stratified split.
- **How it works:** each tree trains on a bootstrap sample and considers a random subset of features at each split; the forest votes. Averaging decorrelated trees reduces variance.
- **Why selected:** works well on small tabular data, needs little tuning, gives feature importances.
- **Alternative:** Gradient Boosting (available in the code), logistic regression, a neural network. **Why not a neural network:** far too little data.

## Prerequisite graph and topological order

The skill graph has 122 nodes, 123 edges, 24 roots and maximum depth 6, verified acyclic at build time. A topological order guarantees every skill appears after its prerequisites. The planner groups gap skills into phases following that order. **Alternative:** ordering by priority alone, which could schedule React before JavaScript.

## Skill-gap priority score

```
priority = importance × 10            role importance 1–5 (a prerequisite inherits 80% of the skill that needs it)
         + 8   if a core requirement
         + 6   per gap skill it unblocks (capped at 24)
         + 12  if the ATS analysis listed it as missing
         + 4   per level to climb
HIGH ≥ 62   MEDIUM ≥ 40   otherwise LOW
```

The weights are a stated design choice, not learned values. Each gap is returned with the reasons that produced its score.

## Item-based collaborative filtering (skill recommender)

```
similarity(i, j) = cooccurrence(i, j) / ( sqrt(count_i × count_j) + shrinkage )      shrinkage = 5
score(candidate) = Σ similarity(candidate, s)  over the skills s the student has
```

Trained on 844 skill "baskets" extracted from real job descriptions and resumes. It beat a popularity baseline and a PPMI + SVD embedding model. **It is not wired into a live feature**: the agent that used it was removed. Its co-occurrence data is reused read-only as job-demand evidence when the career knowledge base is built.

## Judge comparator and verdict classification

Both the expected and the returned value are parsed as JSON and compared structurally, so spacing, trailing newlines or `5` versus `5.0` cannot change a verdict. Floating-point answers use a relative tolerance of 1e-6. A problem may declare `unordered` or `unorderedNested` comparison (for example Two Sum, Subsets). The verdict rule is a fixed decision list (see the DSA module).

# How the AI models are trained

## Beginner: what is an LLM?

A large language model is a neural network trained to predict the next token (a word piece) given the text so far. It has seen a very large amount of text, so it can continue a prompt in a way that reads sensibly. It does not look facts up; it generates what is statistically likely.

## Intermediate: what is fine-tuning?

Fine-tuning continues training a pre-trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset so it behaves the way a task needs — here, producing a strict JSON structure for an ATS assessment or a career plan.

## Advanced: the terms you must be able to define

| Term | Definition | Simple example |
|---|---|---|
| SFT (supervised fine-tuning) | Training on input → target pairs | Resume in, the expected JSON assessment out |
| PEFT | Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: train a small number of extra parameters and freeze the rest | Adding sticky notes to a textbook instead of rewriting it |
| LoRA | Low-Rank Adaptation: for a weight matrix W, learn two small matrices A and B and use `W + (α/r)·B·A` | A 4096×4096 matrix has ~16.8M numbers; with rank 16, A and B together have ~131K |
| QLoRA | LoRA on a base model stored in 4-bit precision | The same textbook, printed smaller, with the same sticky notes |
| Quantization | Storing weights with fewer bits | 16-bit to 4-bit cuts memory by about four times |
| 4-bit NF4 | A 4-bit format designed for normally distributed weights | Used by bitsandbytes |
| Rank (r) | Width of the adapter matrices; higher means more capacity | r = 16 here |
| Alpha (α) | Scaling of the adapter's contribution | α = 32 here, so the scale is α/r = 2 |
| Batch size | Examples processed per forward pass | 1 or 2 on a T4 |
| Gradient accumulation | Summing gradients over several small batches before updating | 1 × 16 behaves like a batch of 16 |
| Gradient checkpointing | Recomputing activations during the backward pass to save memory | Slower, but fits in memory |
| Learning rate | Step size of each update | 1e-4 here |
| Scheduler | How the learning rate changes over time | Cosine decay after a short warm-up |
| Optimizer | The update rule | `paged_adamw_8bit` |
| Epoch | One pass over the training set | 2 planned |
| Validation | Measuring loss on data not trained on | Used for early stopping |
| Checkpoint | A saved copy of the adapter during training | Every 25 or 50 steps to Google Drive |
| Overfitting | Memorising training data instead of learning the task | Training loss falls while validation loss rises |
| Completion-only loss | Loss computed only on the answer tokens | The model learns the JSON, not to reproduce the resume |

## Full fine-tuning, LoRA and QLoRA compared

![Figure 8. LoRA and QLoRA](../diagrams/08_lora_qlora.png)

| | Full fine-tuning | LoRA | QLoRA (used here) |
|---|---|---|---|
| What is trained | Every weight | Small adapter matrices | Small adapter matrices |
| Base model during training | Updated, 16-bit | Frozen, 16-bit | Frozen, **4-bit** |
| Trainable parameters | 100% (billions) | Around 1% | Around 1% (ATS: about 33 million, ~0.8%) |
| GPU memory | Very high | Moderate | Lowest; fits a free 16 GB T4 |
| Output | A full model copy (gigabytes) | An adapter file | An adapter file |
| Risk of forgetting general ability | Higher | Low | Low |
| Cost | Highest | Low | Lowest, slightly slower per step |

**Why QLoRA was selected:** the only GPU available was a free Colab T4 with 16 GB. Full fine-tuning a 4-billion-parameter model does not fit. QLoRA fits, produces a small adapter that can be versioned and swapped, and leaves the base model untouched so the untuned model can be evaluated for comparison with the adapter disabled.

| Approximate size | 4 billion parameters | 1.7 billion parameters |
| Licence of base | Apache-2.0 | Apache-2.0 |
| Method | QLoRA, r 16, α 32, dropout 0.05, all 7 projection layers | Same |

### Why these base models

- **Open licence.** Both are Apache-2.0, so adapters can be trained and used freely.
- **Size fits the hardware.** A 4B model in 4-bit fits a T4 with sequences of about 3,000 tokens. The career model uses a smaller 1.7B model because its sequences are longer (up to 4,096 tokens) and it only has to organise facts supplied in the prompt.
- **Instruction-tuned.** The ATS base is the non-thinking instruct variant, so it emits JSON without a reasoning block. Qwen3-1.7B is a thinking model; prompts are rendered with thinking disabled and a test confirms the training prompt equals the serving prompt token for token.

No comparison with Llama, Mistral or Gemma was run. Do not claim Qwen is better than them; say it met the licence, size and format requirements.

## ATS fine-tuning pipeline

![Figure 7. Fine-tuning pipeline (both models)](../diagrams/07_training_pipeline.png)

1. **Sources inspected, not assumed.** Three public datasets were downloaded and examined: 4,817 structured resumes (MIT), 6,374 resume–JD pairs (Apache-2.0) and 93,733 pairs (no licence declared).
2. **A provided score was rejected.** One dataset's numeric `ats_score` turned out to be "class band plus noise": within a fit class it correlated with nothing in the text (ρ ≈ −0.001). Only the three-class fit label was kept.
3. **Cleaning and privacy.** Unicode normalisation, PII scrub (emails, phones, profile links replaced with placeholders), quality filter, exact de-duplication.
4. **Near-duplicate clustering.** MinHash (64 permutations) with LSH (16 bands), verified by exact Jaccard ≥ 0.8: 6,063 unique resumes became 5,346 clusters; 659 JDs became 382 clusters.
5. **Split before sampling, by cluster.** Resume clusters are assigned to train, validation, test or human review; JD clusters to train or held-out. A pair is usable only when both agree. The leakage audit reports 0 / 0 / 0 and the build refuses to write otherwise.
6. **Weak labels.** Every target is a documented deterministic function built on the existing ATS engine. **No label is produced by an LLM, and none is a human score.**
7. **Truncate before labelling**, so the model is never trained to cite a skill it cannot see.
8. **Training** in the Colab notebook with the settings in the table above.
9. **Evaluation** on three separate axes: teacher fidelity, external validity against fit labels on unseen JDs, and human agreement (not available until the review sheet is filled).
10. **Serving safety.** JSON extraction, strict schema, grounding guard, one corrective retry, then the deterministic engine.

**The model predicts component scores and evidence only. The final ATS score is always computed in Python from fixed weights; a score the model emits is discarded.**

## Career model fine-tuning pipeline

1. **Knowledge base.** 122 skills, 214 aliases, 123 prerequisite links, 20 roles. O*NET 31.0 and ESCO v1.2.1 corroborate which skills belong to a role; they contain no prerequisites, study hours or projects, so those layers are hand-written and are editorial judgement.
2. **Examples.** A synthetic learner profile is passed through the deterministic planner; the plan becomes the target. 10,000 generated, 9,916 kept (84 exceeded 4,096 tokens).
3. **Split by learner profile.** Train 7,157, validation 957, test 1,802. Two roles — Site Reliability Engineer and Product Analyst — never appear in training, to test generalisation to an unseen role.
4. **Facts in the prompt.** Requirements, gaps with hours and priorities, prerequisite links and candidate resource IDs are supplied. The model explains and organises; it does not need to recall a requirement or a URL.
5. **Training run v1.** 591 examples, 1 epoch, 37 learning updates, 82 minutes on a T4, final validation loss 0.273.
6. **Result.** Not usable — see the evaluation chapter.

> **What this training teaches, honestly.** The targets come from a rule-based planner, so the model learns to reproduce that planner's reasoning in fluent form. It can be measured for validity and faithfulness to the supplied facts. It cannot be shown to give *better* career advice than the planner it learned from.

## Inference and fallback

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| Model provider is `none` (current setting) | The deterministic engine or planner answers |
| Model returns valid, grounded JSON | The answer is used; scores are still recomputed in code |
| JSON invalid or fails the schema | One corrective retry showing the model its error |
| Still invalid, timeout, crash or out of memory | The deterministic result is returned, marked `degraded` with the reason |
| Model names a skill not in the resume as matched | Moved to missing and counted |
| Model names a resource ID not in the catalogue | Dropped and counted |

# Evaluation framework

## Choosing the right metric

Accuracy is only meaningful for classification. Three kinds of quality must be kept apart.

| Kind | Question | Examples here |
|---|---|---|
| MODEL QUALITY | Is the model's output correct? | F1 for the classifier; JSON validity and hallucination rate for an LLM |
| SYSTEM QUALITY | Does the pipeline behave correctly? | Tests passing, verdict correctness, fallback behaviour |
| USER EXPERIENCE | Is it useful to a student? | Human ratings — none collected yet |

## Formulas

```
Accuracy  = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)        share of all predictions that are correct
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)                          of what was predicted positive, how much was right
Recall    = TP / (TP + FN)                          of what was truly positive, how much was found
F1        = 2 × Precision × Recall / (Precision + Recall)
MAE       = mean |predicted − target|               average size of a score error
Spearman ρ                                          agreement of rankings, from −1 to +1
MRR       = mean (1 / rank of the correct item)
Recall@K  = share of cases where the correct item is in the top K
```

| Metric | Use it when | Do not use it when |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | Classes are balanced | Classes are imbalanced — a model predicting the majority looks good |
| Precision | False positives are costly (recommending a skill that is not needed) | You need to know what was missed |
| Recall | False negatives are costly (missing a real skill) | You need to know how much noise was added |
| F1 | You need one number balancing both | Costs of the two errors differ greatly |
| MAE, Spearman | The output is a score or a ranking | The output is a category |
| JSON validity, hallucination rate | The output is generated structured text | — |

## Measured — ATS deterministic baselines

Source: `careerpilot_ats/evaluation/metrics.json`. Test split of 485 records (263 general, 222 job-match). "Teacher fidelity" compares a system's score with the weak label. "Versus fit label" compares with a dataset label that no system sees at test time, on job descriptions never seen in training.

| System | Mode | MAE | RMSE | Pearson | Spearman | Spearman vs fit label |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Predict the training mean (trivial floor) | General | 7.50 | 10.31 | — | — | — |
| Predict the training mean (trivial floor) | Job match | 10.96 | 13.37 | — | — | — |
| Existing rule-based engine | General | 5.18 | 5.97 | 0.941 | 0.873 | — |
| Existing engine (keyword coverage) | Job match | 24.86* | 27.93* | 0.823 | 0.795 | 0.079 |
| Rubric heuristic without label anchoring | Job match | 4.05 | 5.13 | 0.948 | 0.942 | 0.227 |
| Base Qwen3-4B | Both | [NOT YET MEASURED] | | | | |
| Fine-tuned Qwen3-4B | Both | [NOT YET MEASURED] | | | | |

\* Different scale: keyword coverage is not a 0–100 fit score, so its MAE is not comparable; its rank correlations are.

**Meaning.** These describe how closely the *rule-based* engine follows the documented rubric (weak labels). They are not accuracy against human judgement. The key finding is that plain keyword coverage barely tracks job fit on unseen jobs (ρ = 0.079), which is the headroom a fine-tuned model would have to beat (ρ = 0.227 for the richer heuristic).

**Human agreement:** [NOT YET MEASURED]. `careerpilot_ats/dataset/careerpilot_human_review.csv` holds 476 examples with empty score columns. Evaluation required before claiming this metric.
