# Performance and speed

No latency, throughput or load benchmark exists in the repository. The table lists the techniques that are actually in the code and marks every one as unmeasured. **Do not quote a speed-up number.**

| Technique | Problem it addresses | Where | Measured? | Expected benefit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Database indexes (about 186 declarations) | Slow lookups by student, slug, status, date | Mongoose schemas | No — performance benchmark required | Indexed queries instead of collection scans |
| Pagination | Large lists | List endpoints (`page`, `limit`) | No | Bounded response size |
| Field selection and `lean()` | Loading whole documents | Services | No | Less data read and serialised |
| `select: false` on hidden tests and solutions | Loading large arrays that are rarely needed | `CodingProblem` | No | Smaller reads; also a security control |
| Route-level code splitting (35 lazy-loaded pages) | Large first download | `React.lazy` in `App.tsx` | No | Smaller initial bundle; Monaco loads only on the problem page |
| Client cache | Repeated identical requests | TanStack Query | No | Fewer round trips |
| Response compression | Payload size | `compression` middleware | No | Smaller responses |
| In-memory configuration cache | Reading weights on every request | `config.service` | No | No database read per readiness computation |
| Docker status cache (20 s) | Checking Docker on every page view | `dockerRunner` | No | One check per 20 seconds |
| Concurrency cap on sandboxes | Host exhaustion under a burst | Semaphore in `codeExecution.service` | No | Bounded resource use; excess requests wait or are refused |
| Compile once per submission | Recompiling for each test | Runner script | No | One compile, many test runs |
| Stop after a time-limit or memory failure | A hanging program occupying a sandbox for every test | Judge | No | Bounded worst-case time per submission |
| Normalised vectors | Computing norms at query time | Embeddings | No | Similarity is one dot product |
| 4-bit quantization (QLoRA) | Model does not fit GPU memory | Training notebooks | Not as a benchmark | Training fits a 16 GB T4 |
| LoRA adapters | Training and storing full model copies | Training notebooks | Not as a benchmark | Around 1% of parameters trained; small adapter file |
| Deterministic engines by default | Slow, costly model calls for every score | ATS, APIE, planner, judge | No | Scores need no GPU and no network |

Not present in the repository: a queue, a Redis-style cache, response streaming, batching of model calls, approximate vector indexes, precomputation jobs.

## Recommended benchmark method

1. **API latency.** Use a load tool (k6 or autocannon) against five endpoints: login, dashboard, problem list, resume analyse, career plan. Report p50, p95 and p99 at 10, 50 and 100 virtual users.
2. **Index effect.** Run the same query with `explain("executionStats")` with and without the index; report documents examined and time.
3. **Judge.** For each language submit a reference solution 50 times; report compile time, per-test time, total time and container start-up overhead; then raise concurrency and report the queue wait.
4. **Frontend.** Lighthouse on the dashboard and the problem page; report bundle sizes with and without code splitting.
5. **Model.** If an adapter is served, report tokens per second, time to a complete JSON answer and GPU memory.

# Novelty, innovation and engineering contribution

Be exact about which word applies. A jury will respect "this is integration and careful engineering" far more than an inflated novelty claim.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| NOVELTY | Something not done before in this form |
| INNOVATION | A new combination or application of known ideas |
| ENGINEERING IMPROVEMENT | A known idea implemented carefully to remove a real weakness |
| FEATURE | A capability users expect; ordinary functionality |

## What the project contributes

| # | Contribution | Category | Existing problem | CareerPilot approach | Benefit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | One readiness engine (APIE) fed by every module | INNOVATION | Scores from separate tools cannot be combined | A weighted, recency-aware, evidence-aware score recomputed after every activity, with human alumni feedback as a bounded modifier | One explainable number and a priority list |
| 2 | "Facts from code, judgement from the model, arithmetic from code" | INNOVATION | LLM-scored systems are unrepeatable and can hallucinate | Models return dimension scores or wording; final scores, matched skills and links come from deterministic code | Scores survive an LLM outage and can be explained |
| 3 | Resource IDs instead of URLs | ENGINEERING IMPROVEMENT | Models invent links | The model may only choose catalogue IDs; unknown IDs are dropped and counted | A hallucinated link cannot reach a student |
| 4 | Hidden tests that never enter the sandbox | ENGINEERING IMPROVEMENT | A naive judge ships expected outputs with the code | Only inputs are streamed, one test at a time; comparison is on the host | Submitted code cannot read the answers |
| 5 | One typed signature generating four language harnesses | ENGINEERING IMPROVEMENT | Per-language problem definitions drift | Starter code and harness are generated from a signature | Adding a language changes no problem |
| 6 | Leakage-controlled dataset construction | ENGINEERING IMPROVEMENT | Near-duplicate resumes leak between train and test | Cluster first, split by cluster, hold out job descriptions, audit and refuse to write on leakage | The test set measures unseen jobs |
| 7 | Honest failure reporting | ENGINEERING IMPROVEMENT | Systems fake a result when a dependency is down | "Not executed", "degraded", "no verified information", provenance labels | Trustworthy outputs |
| 8 | Voice excluded from evaluation | ENGINEERING IMPROVEMENT | Spoken answers can be judged on accent or delivery | The input mode is stored but never sent to the evaluator | Identical words get identical scores |
| 9 | Resume analysis, DSA, interviews, career plan, mentorship in one account | FEATURE (integration) | Students use many tools | One platform | Convenience |
| 10 | Admin screens, CRUD, reports | FEATURE | — | Standard | — |

**What is genuinely novel?** Nothing here is a new algorithm. The honest claim is: *the integration of a single explainable readiness model with a strict separation between deterministic scoring and generative language, applied to campus placement.* Rows 1 and 2 are the ones to lead with.

**What to avoid claiming:** that the ATS model is "AI-powered" in the sense of a trained LLM (it is rule-based today); that the career plan is "AI-generated" by a fine-tuned model (the planner generates it); that any accuracy figure reflects real students.

# Comparison with conventional platforms

Compared with a *conventional single-purpose platform* in each category. Many commercial products combine several of these; the table describes the typical single-purpose tool, not a specific competitor.

| Capability | Typical job portal | Typical resume checker | Typical learning platform | Typical DSA platform | CareerPilot AI |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Resume analysis | Limited | Yes | No | No | Yes, with a nine-criterion breakdown |
| JD comparison | Sometimes | Often | No | No | Yes, predefined or custom |
| Career guidance | Limited | No | Course suggestions | No | Skill-gap based plan |
| Skill gap vs a role | No | Sometimes | Sometimes | No | Yes, with priorities and reasons |
| Roadmap with schedule | No | No | Learning paths | Study plans | Yes, time-feasible |
| Learning resources | No | No | Own catalogue | Editorials | Verified catalogue + videos |
| DSA practice with a judge | No | No | Sometimes | Yes, far larger problem sets | Yes, 28 problems |
| Mock interview | No | No | Sometimes | Sometimes | Yes, text and voice |
| Combined readiness score | No | No | No | No | Yes (prototype weights) |
| Alumni mentorship | No | No | No | No | Yes |
| Institutional analytics | Recruiter-side | No | Sometimes | Sometimes | Yes, placement-side |

**Where CareerPilot is weaker:** a dedicated DSA site has thousands of problems, a hardened production judge and contest features; a dedicated learning platform has far more content. CareerPilot's value is the connection between modules, not depth in any single one.

# Limitations and future work

## Current limitations

| Area | Limitation |
|---|---|
| ATS LLM | Not trained. No adapter exists; no LLM result may be quoted |
| Career LLM | v1 trained on 591 examples for 37 updates; 0% of plans were fully valid; switched off |
| APIE | Weights and band thresholds are design choices, not validated on real placements |
| ML classifier | Trained and evaluated on synthetic data only |
| Embeddings | The default is lexical (feature hashing), not semantic |
| Skill extraction | Finds only the 107 taxonomy skills; no OCR for scanned resumes |
| LLM provider | The local configuration uses the mock provider, which is not a language model |
| DSA sandbox | Not yet executed on a machine with Docker; isolation is unverified there |
| DSA scale | 28 hand-written problems; no queue; no admin problem editor; C not supported; no custom input |
| Sandbox hardening | Docker's default seccomp profile; container isolation is not a VM boundary |
| Career knowledge | Levels, hours and prerequisites written by one author; not reviewed by placement staff |
| Resources | 10 skills have no usable resource; videos are search results that passed an availability check, not quality-reviewed |
| Human evaluation | The ATS review sheet and the career plan review sheet are empty |
| Data | Training resumes are mostly US-style, not Indian campus resumes |
| Performance | No benchmark has been run |
| Security | No multi-factor authentication; no dedicated prompt-injection filter |
| Operations | No CI pipeline, monitoring or cloud deployment in the repository |
| Roles | Recruiter is reserved but not built |

## Future enhancements

All items below are [PLANNED].

1. Train the ATS model on a GPU and record the comparison against the deterministic baselines.
2. Run the career model at `medium` size (about 375 updates) and compare with v1.
3. Collect human scores from placement officers and report agreement.
4. Collect real placement outcomes, validate APIE weights and retrain the classifier.
5. Install Docker, run `npm run judge:verify`, then add a queue with judge workers and a stricter seccomp profile.
6. Add an admin problem editor, more problems, custom test input and C support.
7. Switch to semantic embeddings and evaluate retrieval quality.
8. Add Indian campus resumes with consent and recalibrate.
9. Add CI, monitoring, load testing and a recruiter module.

# End-to-end demo script

## Before you start

- Run `npm run dev` and open `http://localhost:5173`. Confirm all three services are up.
- Demo accounts (password `Demo@Pass123`): `student@careerpilot.demo`, `alumni@careerpilot.demo`, `officer@careerpilot.demo`, `admin@careerpilot.demo`. Confirm each logs in before the session.
- Have one resume PDF and one job description (text or file) ready.
- **Docker:** if Docker Desktop is not installed and the judge image is not built, Run and Submit on DSA problems will say "your code was not run". Decide beforehand whether to show that honestly or to install Docker and run `npm run judge:build` and `npm run judge:verify` first.
- **LLM:** the local setting is `AI_PROVIDER=mock`. Interview questions and written feedback will be marked as mock output. Say so if asked.

## Screen-by-screen

| # | Screen | What to show | What to say | Technical explanation | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Login | Sign in as the student | "Access is role-based; this account can only see its own data." | bcrypt password check, 15-minute JWT, refresh token in an httpOnly cookie with rotation | Security is the base of everything else |
| 2 | Dashboard | Readiness score, component cards, DSA progress, next action | "One score built from seven components, updated after every activity." | APIE: recency weighting, weighted sum, bounded modifiers, bands | The student sees what to fix first |
| 3 | Profile | Skills, CGPA, target companies and roles | "Targets drive the gap analysis and job matching." | `StudentProfile` with arrays of target ids | Personalisation needs a profile |
| 4 | Resume & ATS | Upload a PDF | "The resume is parsed and scored with nine transparent criteria." | PyMuPDF extraction, section detection, taxonomy skill matching, capped rule-based scoring | Explainable, repeatable, no GPU |
| 5 | Resume & ATS | Choose "My own job description", paste or upload a JD, analyse | "Matched and missing skills come from exact matching, not a guess." | JD keywords canonicalised; coverage = matched ÷ total | Shows what to add for a specific job |
| 6 | Job Matching | Pick a company and role | "Eligibility is a hard gate; the score cannot override a CGPA cut-off." | 0.55 required + 0.20 preferred + 0.15 similarity + 0.10 eligibility | Mirrors real screening |
| 7 | Assessments | Start one, refresh mid-test | "The timer lives on the server; the page recovers after a refresh." | Server-stored deadline, autosave, server-side grading | Fairness and reliability |
| 8 | DSA Practice | Filter by tag, open Two Sum, switch language | "The student writes only the function. Starter code for four languages comes from one signature." | Code generation from a typed signature | Extensible by design |
| 9 | DSA Practice | Run, then Submit | "Run uses public tests. Submit adds hidden tests whose inputs are never shown." | One container per submission; expected outputs stay on the host; deterministic verdict | Trustworthy verdicts, safe execution |
| 10 | DSA Practice | Results tab | "Execution Result is from the judge. Static Code Analysis is advisory AI and cannot change the verdict." | Verdict stored before the review is requested | AI does not decide correctness |
| 11 | AI Interview | Answer two questions | "Difficulty adapts to my recent scores, and each answer gets five dimension scores." | Threshold controller; overall recomputed in code with mode weights | Adaptive practice with explainable feedback |
| 12 | Readiness | Component breakdown, ML second opinion | "The rule-based score and a Random Forest prediction are shown side by side, labelled as a prototype." | APIE plus a classifier trained on synthetic data | Honest about what is validated |
| 13 | Career Plan | Pick a role, set hours, generate | "Gaps are prioritised with reasons, ordered by prerequisites, and fitted to my time." | Skill graph, priority score, feasibility scheduling, verified resources by ID | A plan that can actually be followed |
| 14 | Career Plan | Resources tab | "Every link was checked; videos come from the YouTube API." | Catalogue of 270 resources with verification status | No invented links |
| 15 | Alumni | Request a mentor | "Mentors are ranked by company, role and skill overlap." | Weighted match formula; WebRTC room; feedback feeds APIE | Human in the loop |
| 16 | Officer login | Cohort analytics, at-risk list | "Placement staff see who needs help before results arrive." | MongoDB aggregation pipelines | Institutional value |
| 17 | Admin login | Users, AI usage, APIE weights, audit log | "Weights are configurable and every sensitive action is audited." | `SystemConfiguration`, `AuditLog`, weights validated to sum to 1.0 | Governance |

## If something fails during the demo

| Failure | What to say |
|---|---|
| DSA Run says "not executed" | "The sandbox needs Docker on this machine. The system refuses to guess a verdict; it never runs student code on the server as a fallback." |
| AI features fail | "The AI service is a separate process. Scores still work because they are deterministic; only wording degrades." |
| A page is slow | "Analysis runs synchronously in this prototype; a queue is planned." |

# Five-minute presentation

Speak at a steady pace; each block is about 70 to 130 words.

## 0:00 – 0:30  Problem

"A student preparing for placement uses one tool for the resume, another for coding, another for aptitude and another for interviews. None of them share information. So the student cannot answer two simple questions: how ready am I overall, and what should I fix first? The placement cell has the same blind spot across the whole batch."

## 0:30 – 1:00  Existing limitations

"Single-purpose tools give isolated scores. Many resume checkers return a number without explaining it. And AI-only tools can produce different answers for the same input, or invent facts. For something that affects a student's confidence, a score has to be explainable and repeatable."

## 1:00 – 1:30  Proposed solution

"CareerPilot AI puts the whole preparation journey on one account: resume analysis, job matching, assessments, DSA practice, mock interviews, a career plan and alumni mentorship. One engine, which we call APIE, combines all the evidence into a single Placement Readiness Score and tells the student what to work on next."

## 1:30 – 2:30  Architecture

"There are three services. A React and TypeScript frontend. A Node.js and Express gateway that handles authentication, role-based access, MongoDB and real-time events. And a Python FastAPI service that holds the AI: eleven agents, the resume parser, the scoring engines, retrieval and machine learning. The browser never talks to the AI service; only the gateway does, with an internal key. Student code for DSA problems runs in a separate isolated Docker container, never on the server."

## 2:30 – 3:30  AI and ML

"Our design rule is: facts from code, judgement from the model, arithmetic from code. The ATS score is nine rule-based criteria. The readiness score is a weighted model. A language model writes interview questions and scores answers on five dimensions, but the final score is recomputed in code. We also built QLoRA fine-tuning pipelines for two Qwen models. I want to be accurate here: the ATS model has not been trained yet, and the first career model we trained was measured and found not usable, so both are switched off. The product runs on the deterministic engines."

## 3:30 – 4:15  Key functionality

"Three things to notice in the demo. First, resume analysis with a comparison against any job description, showing exactly which skills are missing. Second, the DSA environment: four languages, hidden test cases that never enter the sandbox, and a deterministic verdict. Third, the career plan: skill gaps prioritised with reasons, ordered by prerequisites, fitted to the time the student has, with verified resources."

## 4:15 – 4:45  Innovation

"We do not claim a new algorithm. Our contribution is a single explainable readiness model fed by every module, and a strict separation between deterministic scoring and generative language. A language model here cannot set a score, cannot invent a link, and cannot decide whether code is correct."

## 4:45 – 5:00  Results and future scope

"The platform is tested across all three services, and every one of our 28 reference solutions is accepted in all four languages. Next we will train and evaluate the models on a GPU, validate the readiness weights with real placement outcomes, and collect human ratings. Thank you."

# Ten-minute technical presentation

| Time | Section | Speaking points |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00 – 0:45 | Problem | Preparation is spread over disconnected tools. No overall readiness view for the student or the placement cell. Unexplained scores reduce trust. |
| 0:45 – 1:30 | Existing system | Single-purpose resume checkers, coding sites and learning platforms. Each is good at one thing; none combine the evidence. AI-only scoring is not repeatable. |
| 1:30 – 2:15 | Proposed system | One platform, four roles (student, alumni, placement officer, administrator). One readiness engine fed by every scored activity. |
| 2:15 – 3:30 | Architecture | React + TypeScript SPA. Node.js + Express gateway: JWT, RBAC, Zod validation, MongoDB with 33 models, Socket.IO, 135 endpoints. Python FastAPI AI service: 11 agents and an orchestrator. One trust boundary: only the gateway calls the AI service. Docker Compose for deployment. |
| 3:30 – 4:30 | Modules | Resume and ATS; job matching; assessments with a server-side timer; DSA judge; AI interview with voice; APIE readiness; career plan; mentorship; analytics and PDF reports. |
| 4:30 – 5:30 | Algorithms | Dictionary skill extraction with custom boundaries. Capped multi-criteria ATS scoring. Feature-hashing embeddings and cosine similarity. RAG with a relevance threshold. Harmonic recency weighting in APIE. Random Forest. A prerequisite graph in topological order for the plan. Structural JSON comparison in the judge. |
| 5:30 – 6:30 | AI models | LLM behind a provider interface; mock provider for offline use. Random Forest trained on synthetic data, accuracy 0.735, labelled a prototype. Two QLoRA pipelines: Qwen3-4B for ATS (not trained), Qwen3-1.7B for career plans (v1 not usable). |
| 6:30 – 7:15 | Training | QLoRA: frozen 4-bit base model plus rank-16 adapters, about 1% of parameters. ATS data: three public datasets inspected, PII scrubbed, near-duplicates clustered, split by cluster with a leakage audit, weak labels from the existing engine. Career data: synthetic profiles through the planner, two roles held out. |
| 7:15 – 8:00 | Evaluation | What is measured: deterministic ATS baselines, the classifier, the skill recommender, career model v1, and the judge with 112 reference programs. What is not: any fine-tuned ATS result, human agreement, performance benchmarks. State this plainly. |
| 8:00 – 8:30 | Innovation | One explainable readiness model; "facts from code, judgement from the model, arithmetic from code"; resource IDs instead of URLs; hidden tests that never enter the sandbox. |
| 8:30 – 9:00 | Security | bcrypt, JWT with refresh rotation and family revocation, RBAC, Zod and sanitisation, rate limits, upload magic-byte checks, audit log. Student code only in an isolated container with no network, read-only filesystem, non-root user and resource limits. |
| 9:00 – 9:30 | Performance | Indexes, pagination, lazy-loaded routes, client caching, concurrency cap on sandboxes. No benchmark yet; method defined. |
| 9:30 – 10:00 | Demo pointer and future work | Train and evaluate the models; validate weights with real outcomes; human ratings; verify the sandbox with Docker; queue and admin problem editor. |

## Lines worth memorising

- "Deterministic algorithms compute every score; language models are used only for language."
- "The model reasons; the application knows."
- "A language model here cannot set a score, cannot invent a link, and cannot decide whether code is correct."
- "The accuracy figure is on synthetic data. It shows the pipeline works, not that it predicts real placements."
- "When the sandbox is unavailable the system says 'not executed'. It never guesses a verdict."

# Viva questions and answers

104 questions in 24 groups. Each has a **short** answer (one breath), a **technical** answer, a **deep** answer for a follow-up, and the **common mistake** to avoid.

## A. Basic project questions

**Q1. What is CareerPilot AI?**
- **Short:** A placement-preparation platform that combines resume analysis, coding practice, mock interviews and a career plan into one readiness score.
- **Technical:** A React frontend, a Node.js/Express gateway with MongoDB, and a Python FastAPI AI service with 11 agents.
- **Deep:** Every scored activity triggers APIE, a weighted, recency-aware engine, to recompute a Placement Readiness Score with components, reasons and next actions.
- **Common mistake:** Calling it "an AI that predicts placement". It measures preparation; it does not predict outcomes.

**Q2. What problem does it solve?**
- **Short:** Preparation tools are disconnected, so students cannot see overall readiness or priorities.
- **Technical:** It integrates the evidence from each stage into one explainable score and one plan.
- **Deep:** The placement cell gets the same data as cohort analytics and an at-risk list.
- **Common mistake:** Listing features instead of stating the problem.

**Q3. Who are the users?**
- **Short:** Students, alumni, placement officers and administrators.
- **Technical:** Four active roles enforced by `authorize(role)` middleware; a recruiter role is reserved but not built.
- **Deep:** Each role has its own dashboard and route set; ownership checks stop a student reading another student's data.
- **Common mistake:** Mentioning faculty or recruiters as working roles.

**Q4. What is your one-line technical summary?**
- **Short:** Deterministic algorithms compute every score; language models are used only for language.
- **Technical:** Model outputs are schema-validated and final scores are recomputed from fixed weights.
- **Deep:** This makes scores repeatable, explainable and available even when the LLM is down.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "everything is AI-powered".

**Q5. Which parts actually use a language model today?**
- **Short:** Interview questions, answer evaluation, and the advisory code review.
- **Technical:** Through a provider interface; the local setting is the mock provider.
- **Deep:** The ATS score, readiness score, job match, career plan and judge verdicts use no LLM at all.
- **Common mistake:** Claiming the ATS score or career plan comes from a fine-tuned LLM.

## B. Architecture

**Q6. Why three services?**
- **Short:** Node is good at web I/O; Python has the ML libraries.
- **Technical:** The gateway handles auth, sockets and the database; FastAPI hosts NLP, scoring and ML.
- **Deep:** A shared TypeScript package keeps frontend and backend types identical; the gateway is the single AI caller so auth and audit live in one place.
- **Common mistake:** Calling it microservices. It is three services with one database.

**Q7. How do the services communicate?**
- **Short:** HTTP and WebSocket from the browser; HTTP with an internal key between gateway and AI service.
- **Technical:** `aiClient` adds the key, retries connection errors and maps failures to typed errors.
- **Deep:** The AI service is not exposed publicly, so the key and model access never reach the browser.
- **Common mistake:** Saying the frontend calls the AI service.

**Q8. Is it monolithic or microservices?**
- **Short:** Service-oriented with three services.
- **Technical:** No service discovery, message bus or per-service database.
- **Deep:** The split follows technology and trust boundaries, not team or scaling boundaries.
- **Common mistake:** Over-claiming microservices.

**Q9. What happens if the AI service is down?**
- **Short:** Scores still work in principle because they are deterministic; AI-dependent calls return a clear error.
- **Technical:** The gateway returns `AI_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE`; the resume is saved and can be re-analysed.
- **Deep:** The test suite points the AI client at a closed port to prove graceful degradation.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "nothing breaks". Analysis that needs the Python engine cannot run without it.

**Q10. Where is the single source of truth for types?**
- **Short:** The `shared` package.
- **Technical:** Enums, DTOs and constants imported by both TypeScript apps.
- **Deep:** A change to a DTO breaks the build on both sides, so drift is caught at compile time.
- **Common mistake:** Not knowing the package exists.

## C. Frontend

**Q11. Why React with TypeScript?**
- **Short:** Component reuse and type safety.
- **Technical:** Vite for builds, Tailwind and Radix primitives for UI.
- **Deep:** Types come from the shared package, so API shapes are checked at compile time.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "because it is popular".

**Q12. How is state managed?**
- **Short:** TanStack Query for server data, Zustand for auth.
- **Technical:** Queries are cached by key and invalidated after mutations.
- **Deep:** Separating server state from client state avoids a large global store.
- **Common mistake:** Saying Redux.

**Q13. How is the bundle kept small?**
- **Short:** Route-level code splitting.
- **Technical:** 35 pages are loaded with `React.lazy`; Monaco loads only on the problem page.
- **Deep:** No size benchmark was run; the benefit is expected, not measured.
- **Common mistake:** Quoting a load-time number.

**Q14. Why Monaco?**
- **Short:** It is the editor behind VS Code.
- **Technical:** Syntax highlighting for all four languages; read-only while a run is pending.
- **Deep:** Drafts are saved per problem and language in local storage.
- **Common mistake:** Claiming IntelliSense for user code.

**Q15. How does voice input work?**
- **Short:** The browser's Web Speech API, on the device.
- **Technical:** Speech becomes an editable transcript; `speechSynthesis` reads questions aloud.
- **Deep:** A server Whisper fallback exists behind a provider setting; the input mode is not sent to the evaluator.
- **Common mistake:** Saying audio is analysed for tone or emotion. It is not.

## D. Backend

**Q16. Why Express?**
- **Short:** A mature, simple middleware model.
- **Technical:** Each route is a chain: authenticate, authorize, validate, controller.
- **Deep:** Controllers stay thin; services hold the rules; this keeps logic testable.
- **Common mistake:** Putting business logic in controllers when describing it.

**Q17. How are requests validated?**
- **Short:** Zod schemas.
- **Technical:** `validate({ body, query, params })` rejects bad input with field-level details.
- **Deep:** A sanitiser also strips MongoDB operator keys to prevent NoSQL injection.
- **Common mistake:** Saying validation is only on the frontend.

**Q18. How are errors handled?**
- **Short:** One central error handler.
- **Technical:** `ApiError` carries a status and a machine-readable code.
- **Deep:** Stack traces are logged with pino, not returned to the client.
- **Common mistake:** Saying errors are just `console.log`.

**Q19. How do you log?**
- **Short:** Structured JSON logs with pino.
- **Technical:** Each request has an id; AI calls are recorded in `AIInteraction`.
- **Deep:** Sensitive actions are written to an audit log that administrators can read.
- **Common mistake:** Claiming a monitoring stack. There is none.

**Q20. How do real-time updates work?**
- **Short:** Socket.IO.
- **Technical:** The server emits notifications and `readiness:updated`.
- **Deep:** The same channel carries WebRTC signalling for the alumni interview room.
- **Common mistake:** Saying polling.

## E. Database

**Q21. Why MongoDB?**
- **Short:** The data is nested and changed shape during development.
- **Technical:** Analyses, snapshots and plans are documents; 33 Mongoose models.
- **Deep:** The cost is weaker referential integrity, handled in the service layer.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "NoSQL is faster".

**Q22. How are relationships stored without foreign keys?**
- **Short:** `ObjectId` references.
- **Technical:** Mongoose `populate` resolves them.
- **Deep:** Many-to-many relations use a join document, for example `CodingSubmission` between student and problem.
- **Common mistake:** Saying MongoDB has foreign keys.

**Q23. Why are readiness records append-only?**
- **Short:** To keep history.
- **Technical:** Each computation is a new snapshot with the weights used.
- **Deep:** Old scores stay interpretable after an administrator changes the weights.
- **Common mistake:** Saying the score is overwritten.

**Q24. How are hidden test cases protected in the database?**
- **Short:** They are excluded from queries by default.
- **Technical:** `select: false` on `hiddenTestCases` and `referenceSolutions`.
- **Deep:** Only the Submit path asks for them by name, and the DTO builder never reads them.
- **Common mistake:** Saying they are "filtered out in the frontend".

**Q25. Which indexes matter?**
- **Short:** Lookups by student, slug, status and date.
- **Technical:** About 186 index declarations, including unique `email` and `slug`.
- **Deep:** Their effect has not been benchmarked.
- **Common mistake:** Quoting a query time.

## F. APIs

**Q26. How many endpoints are there?**
- **Short:** 135 under `/api/v1`.
- **Technical:** In 15 route files mounted on 19 paths.
- **Deep:** The AI service has a separate internal API.
- **Common mistake:** Guessing a number.

**Q27. What does a response look like?**
- **Short:** A common envelope.
- **Technical:** `{ success, data, meta }` or `{ success: false, error: { code, message, details } }`.
- **Deep:** Error codes are shared constants, so the frontend can branch on them.
- **Common mistake:** Saying raw objects are returned.

**Q28. Which endpoint analyses a resume?**
- **Short:** `POST /api/v1/resumes/:id/analyze`.
- **Technical:** Optional `jobDescriptionId` or `jobDescriptionText`, never both.
- **Deep:** A custom JD is used for that analysis only and is not stored.
- **Common mistake:** Inventing `/api/resume/analyze`.

**Q29. Run versus Submit?**
- **Short:** Run uses public tests and stores nothing; Submit adds hidden tests and stores the result.
- **Technical:** `POST /coding/problems/:id/run` and `/submit`.
- **Deep:** Only Submit updates readiness and requests the advisory review.
- **Common mistake:** Saying Run also uses hidden tests.

**Q30. Is the API versioned?**
- **Short:** Yes, `/api/v1`.
- **Technical:** The prefix is configuration.
- **Deep:** A breaking change would be released as `/api/v2` beside it.
- **Common mistake:** Saying there is no versioning.

## G. AI and ML

**Q31. What ML model is trained and in use?**
- **Short:** A Random Forest readiness classifier.
- **Technical:** 300 trees, 14 features, four classes.
- **Deep:** Trained on 2,000 synthetic rows; accuracy 0.735, macro F1 0.737, three-fold CV 0.739 ± 0.020.
- **Common mistake:** Presenting 73.5% as accuracy on real students.

**Q32. Why synthetic data?**
- **Short:** There are no real placement outcomes yet.
- **Technical:** Students are drawn from four ability archetypes with Gaussian noise and 6% label flips.
- **Deep:** Noise is added on purpose; without it the labels would be a clean function of the features and accuracy would be about 99% and meaningless.
- **Common mistake:** Hiding that it is synthetic.

**Q33. Why Random Forest?**
- **Short:** It suits small tabular data.
- **Technical:** Little tuning, handles mixed scales, gives feature importances.
- **Deep:** Gradient Boosting is available as an alternative; a neural network would overfit this little data.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "it has the best accuracy" without a comparison.

**Q34. What are the top features?**
- **Short:** Academic, coding and technical scores.
- **Technical:** Importances 0.191, 0.157, 0.151.
- **Deep:** These are global importances, not a per-student explanation such as SHAP.
- **Common mistake:** Calling them causal.

**Q35. What is the difference between APIE and the classifier?**
- **Short:** APIE is a rule-based score; the classifier is a learned second opinion.
- **Technical:** Both read the same components.
- **Deep:** They are shown side by side; APIE is authoritative because it is explainable.
- **Common mistake:** Saying the classifier produces the readiness score.

## H. LLM

**Q36. Which LLM does the project use?**
- **Short:** Any provider behind one interface; the local setting is the mock.
- **Technical:** `AI_PROVIDER` selects OpenAI-compatible, Azure, Ollama or mock.
- **Deep:** The mock is rule-based and tagged `provider: "mock"`; it is not a language model.
- **Common mistake:** Naming a specific model as "the one we use" without checking the setting.

**Q37. How do you control LLM output?**
- **Short:** JSON schemas, low temperature and recomputed scores.
- **Technical:** Pydantic validation on every agent output.
- **Deep:** The model returns dimension scores; the overall comes from fixed weights in code.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "we trust the model".

**Q38. What is a transformer?**
- **Short:** A neural network built on attention.
- **Technical:** Each token attends to others to build a context-aware representation.
- **Deep:** Stacked attention and feed-forward layers; LoRA adapters are attached to their projection matrices.
- **Common mistake:** Confusing it with an RNN.

**Q39. What is tokenization?**
- **Short:** Splitting text into pieces the model reads.
- **Technical:** Sequence limits are in tokens: 3,072 for ATS, 4,096 for the career model.
- **Deep:** Over-long career examples were dropped rather than truncated; ATS text is truncated before labelling.
- **Common mistake:** Saying tokens are words.

**Q40. What is hallucination and how do you handle it?**
- **Short:** A fluent statement with no basis.
- **Technical:** Schemas, a grounding guard, resource IDs and a RAG threshold.
- **Deep:** Facts come from deterministic extraction; a "matched" skill not in the resume is moved to missing and counted.
- **Common mistake:** Claiming hallucination is eliminated.

## I. Fine-tuning

**Q41. Which models did you fine-tune?**
- **Short:** Two pipelines: Qwen3-4B for ATS and Qwen3-1.7B for career plans.
- **Technical:** Both QLoRA, rank 16, alpha 32.
- **Deep:** The ATS model has not been trained; the career model's first run was measured as not usable. Neither is serving.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "we fine-tuned and deployed Qwen".

**Q42. What is supervised fine-tuning?**
- **Short:** Training on input and target pairs.
- **Technical:** Chat-format examples with completion-only loss.
- **Deep:** Loss is computed on the answer tokens only, so the model learns the JSON and not to reproduce the resume.
- **Common mistake:** Confusing it with pre-training.

**Q43. Where do the ATS labels come from?**
- **Short:** Weak labels computed by formulas on the existing engine.
- **Technical:** No label is produced by an LLM or a human.
- **Deep:** Three holistic components are blended with a dataset fit label at λ = 0.35; the rest are pure evidence.
- **Common mistake:** Calling them ground truth.

**Q44. How did you prevent data leakage?**
- **Short:** Split by near-duplicate cluster before sampling.
- **Technical:** MinHash with LSH, verified by Jaccard ≥ 0.8; job descriptions are held out too.
- **Deep:** An audit over all split pairs reports 0/0/0 and the build refuses to write otherwise.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "we used a random split".

**Q45. Why was a dataset's provided ATS score discarded?**
- **Short:** It carried no information beyond the class label.
- **Technical:** Within a class its correlation with text features was about −0.001.
- **Deep:** The three classes sat in disjoint score bands with the same spread: class band plus noise.
- **Common mistake:** Using a provided label without inspecting it.

## J. LoRA

**Q46. What is LoRA?**
- **Short:** Training small adapter matrices instead of the whole model.
- **Technical:** `W' = W + (α/r)·B·A` with W frozen.
- **Deep:** A and B are low-rank, so the number of trained parameters is small.
- **Common mistake:** Saying LoRA compresses the model.

**Q47. What do rank and alpha mean?**
- **Short:** Rank is adapter capacity; alpha scales its effect.
- **Technical:** r = 16, α = 32, so the scale is 2.
- **Deep:** Higher rank can fit more but risks overfitting on small data.
- **Common mistake:** Confusing rank with the number of layers.

**Q48. Which layers have adapters?**
- **Short:** All seven projection layers.
- **Technical:** The attention and feed-forward projections.
- **Deep:** For the ATS model that is about 33 million trainable parameters, about 0.8%.
- **Common mistake:** Quoting a parameter count for the career model; it was not recorded.

**Q49. What is the output of LoRA training?**
- **Short:** A small adapter file.
- **Technical:** `adapter_model.safetensors` and its config.
- **Deep:** The base model is unchanged, so the untuned model can be evaluated by disabling the adapter.
- **Common mistake:** Saying a new full model is produced.

## K. QLoRA

**Q50. What is QLoRA?**
- **Short:** LoRA on a base model loaded in 4-bit.
- **Technical:** 4-bit NF4 quantization with bitsandbytes or Unsloth.
- **Deep:** The frozen weights are quantized; adapters train in higher precision.
- **Common mistake:** Saying the adapters are 4-bit.

**Q51. Why QLoRA and not full fine-tuning?**
- **Short:** Only a free 16 GB T4 was available.
- **Technical:** Full fine-tuning of a 4B model does not fit.
- **Deep:** QLoRA also gives a swappable, versioned adapter and a clean base-versus-tuned comparison.
- **Common mistake:** Saying QLoRA is more accurate.

**Q52. What does quantization cost?**
- **Short:** A small loss of precision.
- **Technical:** Each training step is somewhat slower.
- **Deep:** No quantized-versus-full comparison was run in this project.
- **Common mistake:** Claiming zero quality loss.

**Q53. What is gradient accumulation and why use it?**
- **Short:** Simulating a larger batch on a small GPU.
- **Technical:** 1 × 16 for ATS behaves like batch 16.
- **Deep:** For the career model, updating every 16 examples gave only 37 updates in v1, which is why the notebook now updates every 4.
- **Common mistake:** Saying it speeds training up.

## L. NLP

**Q54. Which NLP techniques are used?**
- **Short:** Regex, dictionary matching and spaCy NER.
- **Technical:** Section detection by heading patterns; skills from a taxonomy.
- **Deep:** The only statistical NLP model in the resume path is spaCy's NER, used for the name.
- **Common mistake:** Claiming TF-IDF or BERT.

**Q55. Why not `\b` word boundaries?**
- **Short:** They break on `C++` and `C#`.
- **Technical:** A custom look-around excludes letters, digits, `+` and `#`.
- **Deep:** It also stops "Java" matching inside "JavaScript"; this is tested.
- **Common mistake:** Saying substring search is used.

**Q56. How are skill variations handled?**
- **Short:** Aliases map to a canonical name.
- **Technical:** 181 aliases for 107 skills, with flexible separators.
- **Deep:** "ReactJS", "React.js" and "react js" all become "React".
- **Common mistake:** Saying fuzzy matching.

**Q57. What if the resume is a scanned image?**
- **Short:** It is rejected with a clear message.
- **Technical:** Fewer than 120 extracted characters raises a parse error.
- **Deep:** OCR is not implemented; it is future work.
- **Common mistake:** Claiming OCR support.

## M. ATS

**Q58. How is the ATS score calculated?**
- **Short:** Nine rule-based criteria summing to 100.
- **Technical:** Skills 20, structure 15, experience 15, contact 10, education 10, impact 10, formatting 10, verbs 5, length 5.
- **Deep:** Each uses capped formulas, giving diminishing returns.
- **Common mistake:** Saying an LLM scores the resume.

**Q59. How do you know the ATS score is accurate?**
- **Short:** It is a transparent rubric, not a validated predictor.
- **Technical:** Against weak labels the engine has MAE 5.18 and Spearman 0.873 in general mode.
- **Deep:** No human agreement exists yet; the review sheet of 476 examples is empty.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "it matches real ATS systems".

**Q60. What was learned from the baseline evaluation?**
- **Short:** Keyword coverage barely tracks job fit on unseen jobs.
- **Technical:** Spearman 0.079 against fit labels; a richer heuristic reaches 0.227.
- **Deep:** That gap is the headroom a fine-tuned model would have to beat.
- **Common mistake:** Claiming the fine-tuned model beat it. It was not measured.

**Q61. If the model were enabled, what would it decide?**
- **Short:** Component scores and wording only.
- **Technical:** The final score is aggregated in Python.
- **Deep:** Matched and missing keywords stay deterministic even then.
- **Common mistake:** Saying the model outputs the ATS score.

## N. Career plan

**Q62. How is the career plan generated?**
- **Short:** By a deterministic planner.
- **Technical:** Normalise skills, find gaps, score priority, order by prerequisites, fit to time.
- **Deep:** A fine-tuned model can optionally reword and organise it; that path is off.
- **Common mistake:** Saying a fine-tuned LLM writes the plan.

**Q63. How is priority decided?**
- **Short:** An additive score with stated weights.
- **Technical:** Importance × 10, +8 core, +6 per skill unblocked, +12 if ATS flagged it, +4 per level.
- **Deep:** HIGH at 62, MEDIUM at 40; each gap returns its reasons.
- **Common mistake:** Saying the weights were learned.

**Q64. How do you ensure a correct learning order?**
- **Short:** A prerequisite graph.
- **Technical:** 122 skills, 123 edges, verified acyclic, topological order.
- **Deep:** A skill is never deferred while a kept skill depends on it.
- **Common mistake:** Saying order is by priority only.

**Q65. What if the deadline is too short?**
- **Short:** Low-priority gaps are deferred, and the plan says so.
- **Technical:** 75/15/10 time budget; defer LOW then MEDIUM secondary gaps.
- **Deep:** If it still does not fit, the plan states the deadline is not achievable at this pace.
- **Common mistake:** Saying the plan always fits.

**Q66. Where does role knowledge come from?**
- **Short:** A curated knowledge base, corroborated by O*NET, ESCO and job postings.
- **Technical:** 81% of 275 role-to-skill links are corroborated.
- **Deep:** Levels, hours and prerequisites are editorial and unvalidated; O*NET and ESCO do not contain them.
- **Common mistake:** Saying the roadmap "comes from O*NET".

## O. Recommendation systems

**Q67. How are resources recommended?**
- **Short:** A deterministic ranking over a verified catalogue.
- **Technical:** Points for covering the skill, stage match, verification, quality weight, preference and language.
- **Deep:** Ties break on the resource ID so the order is reproducible.
- **Common mistake:** Calling it collaborative filtering.

**Q68. Is there a learned recommender?**
- **Short:** Yes, for skills, but it is not live.
- **Technical:** Item-based collaborative filtering with shrinkage.
- **Deep:** Recall@5 0.411 against 0.272 for popularity, with a 95% interval of +0.101 to +0.176.
- **Common mistake:** Presenting it as a running feature.

**Q69. Why did the simpler recommender win?**
- **Short:** The dataset is small.
- **Technical:** 844 baskets; PPMI + SVD embeddings scored lower.
- **Deep:** A popularity penalty was also tested and rejected because it lowered validation scores.
- **Common mistake:** Assuming the more complex model is better.

**Q70. What is `quality_score`?**
- **Short:** An editorial weight by resource type.
- **Technical:** Between 0 and 1.
- **Deep:** It is not a user rating; there is no rating data.
- **Common mistake:** Calling it a rating.

## P. YouTube API

**Q71. Why use the YouTube Data API?**
- **Short:** To get current videos that actually exist.
- **Technical:** Search per skill, keep public and embeddable videos.
- **Deep:** 180 videos are in the catalogue; a live search endpoint returns results labelled unverified.
- **Common mistake:** Saying the model generates YouTube links.

**Q72. What if YouTube returns an irrelevant video?**
- **Short:** It ranks lower or is not used.
- **Technical:** 151 of 180 name the skill in the title; the other 29 rank lower.
- **Deep:** Videos are availability-checked, not quality-reviewed; that is a stated limitation.
- **Common mistake:** Claiming relevance is guaranteed.

**Q73. Where is the API key?**
- **Short:** Only in the local `.env` file.
- **Technical:** Never in code, the example file or the Colab package.
- **Deep:** The packaging script scans the archive for key-shaped strings and fails if it finds one.
- **Common mistake:** Showing the key on screen.

## Q. DSA judge

**Q74. How is submitted code executed?**
- **Short:** In a throw-away Docker container.
- **Technical:** Compile once, then run each test with inputs streamed by the host.
- **Deep:** The harness writes the return value to a result file; the host compares it with the expected value.
- **Common mistake:** Saying code runs on the backend.

**Q75. How is the verdict decided?**
- **Short:** By a fixed decision list.
- **Technical:** Time limit, memory, runtime error, wrong answer, accepted.
- **Deep:** The submission's verdict is its first failing test; no AI is involved.
- **Common mistake:** Saying AI checks the code.

**Q76. How do you compare outputs?**
- **Short:** Structurally, as JSON.
- **Technical:** Float tolerance 1e-6; optional order-insensitive modes.
- **Deep:** Formatting cannot change a verdict because values, not text, are compared.
- **Common mistake:** Saying string comparison.

**Q77. How are four languages supported from one problem?**
- **Short:** Code generation from a typed signature.
- **Technical:** Starter code and harness are generated per language.
- **Deep:** Arguments use a token format that every language can parse without a JSON library.
- **Common mistake:** Saying each problem is written four times.

**Q78. How was the judge tested?**
- **Short:** 28 reference solutions in four languages, all accepted.
- **Technical:** 112 programs on every public and hidden test.
- **Deep:** Through a test-only local transport with local compilers; container isolation was not exercised.
- **Common mistake:** Saying the Docker sandbox was tested.

## R. Docker

**Q79. Why Docker?**
- **Short:** Isolation with resource limits.
- **Technical:** Namespaces and cgroups separate the process and cap memory, CPU and processes.
- **Deep:** It is not a VM boundary; a dedicated host and stricter profiles are recommended for hostile traffic.
- **Common mistake:** Saying Docker is fully secure.

**Q80. How do you stop an infinite loop?**
- **Short:** A time limit.
- **Technical:** `timeout` inside the container and a host-side deadline.
- **Deep:** After a time-limit failure the remaining tests are not run, bounding total time.
- **Common mistake:** Saying the server detects loops.

**Q81. How do you stop a fork bomb?**
- **Short:** A process limit.
- **Technical:** `--pids-limit`.
- **Deep:** The verification script includes a fork-bomb probe.
- **Common mistake:** Saying memory limits handle it.

**Q82. How are memory limits enforced?**
- **Short:** A container ceiling plus per-language limits.
- **Technical:** `-Xmx` for Java, `--max-old-space-size` for Node, an address-space limit for C++.
- **Deep:** C++ and Java containers get a larger ceiling because their compilers need it.
- **Common mistake:** Saying one flag does everything.

**Q83. Why is the judge disabled in Docker Compose?**
- **Short:** A containerised backend would need the host's Docker socket.
- **Technical:** Mounting that socket is root on the host.
- **Deep:** So the backend runs on the host when the judge is needed.
- **Common mistake:** Suggesting the socket be mounted.

## S. Security

**Q84. How are passwords stored?**
- **Short:** As bcrypt hashes.
- **Technical:** 12 rounds with a per-password salt.
- **Deep:** The cost factor makes brute force slow.
- **Common mistake:** Saying encrypted. Hashing is one-way.

**Q85. How does authentication work?**
- **Short:** A short-lived access token and a rotating refresh token.
- **Technical:** 15 minutes and 7 days; refresh in a signed httpOnly cookie.
- **Deep:** Reuse of an old refresh token revokes the whole family.
- **Common mistake:** Saying tokens are stored in the database as sessions.

**Q86. How do you prevent injection?**
- **Short:** Validation and sanitisation.
- **Technical:** Zod types; operator keys stripped.
- **Deep:** Mongoose casts values to schema types as a further layer.
- **Common mistake:** Talking about SQL injection for MongoDB.

**Q87. How are uploads secured?**
- **Short:** Type, content and size checks.
- **Technical:** Extension, MIME type, magic bytes, 5 MB.
- **Deep:** Files are stored under generated keys and served only as attachments.
- **Common mistake:** Saying only the extension is checked.

**Q88. How are resumes protected?**
- **Short:** Owner-only access with audit.
- **Technical:** Ownership checks; staff access is logged.
- **Deep:** Training data was PII-scrubbed; privacy endpoints support export and deletion.
- **Common mistake:** Claiming encryption at rest. Not in the repository.

## T. Performance

**Q89. What performance optimisations exist?**
- **Short:** Indexes, pagination, lazy loading, caching, a concurrency cap.
- **Technical:** See the performance table.
- **Deep:** None has been benchmarked.
- **Common mistake:** Quoting a speed-up.

**Q90. How would you benchmark?**
- **Short:** Load tests and query plans.
- **Technical:** p50/p95/p99 latency at fixed users; `explain("executionStats")`.
- **Deep:** For the judge: compile time, per-test time and queue wait under concurrency.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "it feels fast".

**Q91. What is the bottleneck?**
- **Short:** Synchronous analysis and the judge.
- **Technical:** Both run inside the request.
- **Deep:** A queue with workers is the planned fix.
- **Common mistake:** Saying there is none.

## U. Algorithms

**Q92. What is cosine similarity?**
- **Short:** The angle between two vectors.
- **Technical:** Dot product over the product of norms.
- **Deep:** With normalised vectors it equals the dot product.
- **Common mistake:** Confusing it with Euclidean distance.

**Q93. Do you use TF-IDF?**
- **Short:** No.
- **Technical:** Feature hashing with sub-linear term frequency.
- **Deep:** There is no inverse document frequency term; it is a lexical embedding.
- **Common mistake:** Saying yes.

**Q94. What is RAG?**
- **Short:** Retrieve relevant text, then generate from it.
- **Technical:** Chunk, embed, top-5 search, relevance filter, answer with sources.
- **Deep:** Below the threshold the LLM is not called at all.
- **Common mistake:** Saying RAG removes hallucination.

**Q95. How was the RAG threshold chosen?**
- **Short:** By measurement.
- **Technical:** On-topic 0.28–0.31, adjacent 0.11–0.14, unrelated 0.02–0.07; 0.18 sits in the gap.
- **Deep:** It depends on the embedder, so semantic embedders use 0.25.
- **Common mistake:** Saying it was guessed.

**Q96. Why harmonic recency weighting?**
- **Short:** Recent results matter more, without ignoring history.
- **Technical:** Weights 1, ½, ⅓.
- **Deep:** A mean ignores improvement; latest-only is too noisy.
- **Common mistake:** Saying exponential decay.

## V. Innovation

**Q97. What is novel?**
- **Short:** The integration, not a new algorithm.
- **Technical:** One explainable readiness model fed by every module.
- **Deep:** Plus a strict split between deterministic scoring and generative language.
- **Common mistake:** Calling CRUD or a dashboard an innovation.

**Q98. What is your measurable improvement?**
- **Short:** None measured against another product.
- **Technical:** Internal measurements exist: baselines, classifier, recommender, judge correctness.
- **Deep:** A user study or outcome comparison is future work.
- **Common mistake:** Inventing a percentage.

## W. Limitations

**Q99. What is the biggest limitation?**
- **Short:** Nothing is validated against real placement outcomes.
- **Technical:** Weights are design choices; ML data is synthetic.
- **Deep:** Both fine-tuned models are off; no human evaluation exists.
- **Common mistake:** Saying there are no limitations.

**Q100. Why is the career model not usable?**
- **Short:** Too little training.
- **Technical:** 591 examples, 37 updates; 51.7% valid JSON, 6.7% passed the schema, 0% fully valid.
- **Deep:** 21 of 60 outputs never stopped; loss was still falling when the run ended.
- **Common mistake:** Hiding the result.

**Q101. Is the sandbox verified?**
- **Short:** The logic yes, the container isolation not yet.
- **Technical:** Docker was not installed on the development machine.
- **Deep:** `npm run judge:verify` runs hostile programs to check each control.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "fully tested".

## X. Future scope

**Q102. What is next?**
- **Short:** Train and evaluate the models, and validate the weights.
- **Technical:** GPU runs, human review sheets, real outcome data.
- **Deep:** Then a judge queue, an admin problem editor and semantic embeddings.
- **Common mistake:** Listing unrelated features.

**Q103. How would you validate APIE?**
- **Short:** Against real outcomes.
- **Technical:** Collect placement results, fit weights, compare with the current ones.
- **Deep:** Report calibration and discrimination, and re-validate each year.
- **Common mistake:** Saying "ask students if they like it".

**Q104. How would it scale?**
- **Short:** Stateless services behind a load balancer.
- **Technical:** A queue and judge workers; a shared cache; a managed database.
- **Deep:** Socket.IO would need a shared adapter; none of this is built.
- **Common mistake:** Saying it already scales.

# Questions the jury may ask to challenge the project

Each answer is written to be said aloud. They are honest first and strong second; a jury trusts the second only after hearing the first.

**1. Why did you use an LLM instead of traditional ML?**
We used both, each where it fits. Scores are rule-based or classical ML because they must be repeatable and explainable. An LLM is used only where the task is language: writing an interview question, judging a free-text answer, phrasing advice. Traditional ML cannot generate a follow-up question; an LLM should not be trusted to add up a score.

**2. Why QLoRA instead of full fine-tuning?**
Hardware and risk. The only GPU was a free 16 GB Colab T4, and full fine-tuning of a 4-billion-parameter model does not fit. QLoRA freezes the base model in 4-bit and trains about 1% of the parameters. It also gives a small adapter we can version, and lets us evaluate the untuned base model simply by disabling the adapter.

**3. Why this base model?**
Three requirements: an open licence, a size that fits a T4 at our sequence length, and reliable instruction-following for JSON. Qwen3 met them and is Apache-2.0. We did not benchmark it against Llama, Mistral or Gemma, so we do not claim it is better — only that it met the requirements.

**4. How do you prevent hallucination?**
By not asking the model for facts. Skills come from dictionary extraction, scores from formulas, links from a catalogue. Where a model is used, its output must pass a strict schema; a skill it claims is matched but is not in the resume is moved to missing; a resource ID not in the catalogue is dropped; and RAG refuses to answer below a relevance threshold without calling the model. We reduce and detect hallucination; we do not claim to eliminate it.

**5. How do you calculate the ATS score?**
Nine criteria with fixed maximum points summing to 100: skills 20, section structure 15, experience 15, contact 10, education 10, quantified impact 10, formatting 10, action verbs 5, length 5. Each is a capped formula, so piling up keywords gives diminishing returns. The breakdown is returned with the score.

**6. How do you know the score is accurate?**
We do not claim it predicts a real employer's ATS. It is a transparent rubric. What we measured: against our weak labels the engine has a mean absolute error of 5.18 and rank correlation of 0.873 in general mode. What we have not measured: agreement with human reviewers. A 476-example review sheet exists and is empty.

**7. How do you evaluate a generated career roadmap?**
Not with accuracy, because it is generation, not classification. The evaluator measures 13 things: JSON validity, schema compliance, skill-gap F1 against the deterministic analysis, priority agreement, prerequisite correctness, ordering, role alignment, personalisation, schedule feasibility, resource-ID validity, resource hallucination, contradictions and duplicates. Whether the advice is *good* needs expert rating; that sheet is prepared and not yet filled.

**8. Why not use RAG for everything?**
RAG fits questions answered by documents. A readiness score needs arithmetic, a study plan needs constraint handling, and a code verdict needs execution. Retrieval does none of those. We use RAG where it belongs — the knowledge base — and deterministic code elsewhere.

**9. Why do you need the YouTube API?**
Because a model's knowledge is frozen at training time and videos change. The API returns videos that exist now and tells us whether they are public and embeddable. The model's job is to reason about which skill to study; the API's job is to find current material.

**10. What happens if YouTube returns irrelevant videos?**
Catalogue videos whose title does not name the skill rank lower: 29 of 180 are in that group. Live search results are labelled "unverified" and are never added to the catalogue. Honestly, videos are availability-checked, not quality-reviewed; a human review step is future work.

**11. What happens if the model recommends a broken course?**
It cannot recommend a course directly. It may only choose resource IDs that were supplied in the prompt. Each ID resolves to a catalogue entry that was fetched and verified; an unknown ID is dropped and counted as a hallucination. A link can still go stale after verification, which is why each entry stores when it was last verified.

**12. How do you verify resources?**
Each non-video URL was requested over HTTPS: 88 of 90 verified, 2 excluded. Videos were checked through the YouTube Data API. The verifier itself is hardened against server-side request forgery: HTTPS only, the provider's own domain only, no private or loopback addresses, at most three redirects, and a cap on bytes read.

**13. How do you prevent prompt injection?**
We do not have a dedicated injection filter, and I will not claim one. The defence is structural: the model has no tools, cannot set a final score because scores are recomputed from fixed weights, and anything outside the schema is rejected. So an instruction hidden in a resume can at most distort wording, not a score. A classifier for injected instructions is future work.

**14. How do you protect user resumes?**
Uploads are checked by extension, MIME type and magic bytes; stored under generated keys; and returned only to the owner or, with an audit entry, to staff. Downloads are sent as attachments with `nosniff`. Training data was scrubbed of emails, phones and profile links. Encryption at rest is not implemented in the repository and would be the storage provider's responsibility.

**15. How is user code executed securely?**
In its own container with no network, a read-only filesystem, a non-root user, all capabilities dropped, and limits on memory, CPU, processes and time. No environment variables are passed in, so no secret is present. Expected outputs never enter the container. I should add: this was verified with unit tests and local compilers, but not yet run under Docker on our machine.

**16. Why Docker?**
It is the standard isolation primitive, with namespaces to separate the process and cgroups to cap resources, and containers start quickly. It is not as strong as a virtual machine. For hostile public traffic we would add a dedicated host, a custom seccomp profile or gVisor.

**17. How do you prevent infinite loops?**
A time limit enforced twice: `timeout` inside the container, and a deadline on the host that removes the container if the inner timer fails. After a time-limit failure the remaining tests are skipped, so one submission cannot occupy a sandbox for the whole test set.

**18. How do you handle memory limits?**
The container has a hard memory ceiling with swap disabled. Because compilers need more memory than the problem allows, the per-problem limit is also enforced on the program: `-Xmx` for Java, `--max-old-space-size` for Node, an address-space limit for C++. Exceeding it gives Memory Limit Exceeded.

**19. What happens if the model goes down?**
Scores are unaffected in principle because none is produced by a model. Features that need the AI service return a clear error rather than a fabricated result. For the fine-tuned paths, a timeout or crash falls back to the deterministic engine and marks the response `degraded` with the reason.

**20. What is your fallback architecture?**
Every model has a deterministic twin: the ATS engine behind the ATS model, the planner behind the career model, the mock provider behind the LLM. The order is: valid model answer; else one corrective retry; else the deterministic result, labelled as such. A degraded answer is never presented as a model answer.

**21. What is actually novel?**
No new algorithm. The contribution is integration with discipline: one explainable readiness model fed by every module, and a hard line between deterministic scoring and generative language. Smaller engineering contributions support it — resource IDs instead of URLs, hidden tests that never enter the sandbox, leakage-audited datasets.

**22. What is your measurable improvement?**
I have no measured improvement over another product or over a baseline cohort, and I will not invent one. What is measured is internal: the baselines for the ATS engine, the classifier and recommender metrics, the career model's results, and judge correctness on 112 reference programs. A user study is the next step.

**23. What is the biggest limitation?**
Validation. The readiness weights are a design choice, the classifier is trained on synthetic data, the fine-tuned models are not in service, and no human has rated the outputs. The system is engineered carefully, but its usefulness to real students is not yet demonstrated.

**24. Why should someone use this instead of existing platforms?**
Not for depth in one area — a dedicated coding site has far more problems. The reason is connection: a resume gap changes the career plan, a coding result moves the readiness score, an alumni's feedback adjusts it, and the placement cell sees all of it. That linkage is what a set of separate tools cannot give.

**25. What happens when the job market changes?**
Nothing needs retraining for facts. Role requirements, prerequisites and resources are data files, and the model receives them in the prompt, so a new role or resource works immediately. Two roles were held out of training precisely to test that. What does need periodic human review is the curated knowledge itself.

**26. You say "AI platform", but most of it is rules. Is that not misleading?**
It would be if we hid it. We state it openly: rules compute the scores because scores must be defensible, and AI is used for language. We consider that the right design for a system that judges students, not a weakness.

**27. Your accuracy is only 73.5%. Is that not poor?**
It is on purpose not higher. The data is synthetic with deliberate noise; without the noise the labels would be a clean function of the features and accuracy would be about 99%, which would mean nothing. The figure shows the pipeline works. It says nothing about real placements.

**28. Why did you remove Group Discussion and the earlier roadmap?**
They were removed from the product to focus the scope. The readiness weights were rebalanced — the former 10% went to coding and communication — and stored records were migrated. The career plan replaced the earlier roadmap with a deterministic, testable planner.

**29. Did you write all of this yourself?**
Answer truthfully about your own contribution and the tools you used. Whatever the answer, be able to explain any module from this document: that is what the jury is really checking.

**30. If you had one more month, what would you do first?**
Collect ground truth. Have placement officers score 100 resumes and rate 30 career plans, gather last year's placement outcomes, and then train and evaluate the models against those. Everything else — more problems, a queue, better embeddings — matters less than knowing whether the scores are right.

# Concepts explained like a professor

Each concept: what it is, how CareerPilot uses it, a simple example, and the technical point to add if pressed.

## Web and system concepts

| Concept | Definition | In CareerPilot | Simple example | Technical point |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frontend | The part that runs in the browser | React + TypeScript single-page app | The Resume page you see | Renders from JSON returned by the API |
| Backend | The server-side program | Node.js + Express gateway | Checks your login and saves a submission | Stateless request handling with middleware chains |
| REST API | Resources addressed by URLs and HTTP verbs | 135 endpoints under `/api/v1` | `GET /coding/problems` lists problems | JSON envelope with typed error codes |
| Database | Organised persistent storage | MongoDB with 33 Mongoose models | Your resume analysis is one document | Documents with `ObjectId` references and indexes |
| Authentication | Proving who you are | Email and password, then a token | Logging in | bcrypt comparison, then a signed JWT |
| Authorization | Deciding what you may do | Role middleware and ownership checks | A student cannot open the admin page | `authorize(role)` plus per-record owner check |
| JWT | A signed token carrying claims | 15-minute access token | A wristband that expires | HMAC signature; verified without a database lookup |
| MongoDB | A document database | The only database | A plan stored as one nested document | No joins or foreign keys; references are populated |
| Services (not microservices) | Separate programs with separate jobs | Three: frontend, gateway, AI service | Python does ML, Node does web | One database, no message bus |
| Docker | Packaging and isolating a process | The judge sandbox; Compose for deployment | A sealed box for one run | Namespaces isolate, cgroups limit |
| Container | A running isolated process from an image | One per code submission | The box is thrown away after the run | `--rm`, no network, read-only root |
| API gateway | A single entry point in front of services | The Node backend plays this role | The reception desk | It alone holds the internal AI key |
| Queue | A waiting line for background jobs | **Not used**; an in-process limiter instead | — | A queue with workers is planned |
| Caching | Keeping a result to avoid recomputing | Client query cache; in-memory config cache | Not refetching the problem list | No Redis; server caches are per process |

## AI and NLP concepts

| Concept | Definition | In CareerPilot | Simple example | Technical point |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NLP | Processing human language | Resume parsing and skill extraction | Finding "Python" in a resume | Regex, dictionary matching, spaCy NER |
| Embedding | A vector representing text | 384-dimensional hashed vectors | Two similar texts get nearby vectors | Feature hashing, sub-linear TF, L2-normalised |
| Vector database | A store searched by vector similarity | NumPy store by default; FAISS or Chroma optional | Finding the closest chunks | Exact inner-product search |
| Semantic search | Search by meaning, not exact words | Available by switching the embedder; default is lexical | "car" finding "automobile" | Needs a learned embedding model |
| RAG | Retrieve text, then generate from it | Knowledge-base answers | Answering from the placement handbook | Top-5 retrieval, relevance threshold, sources returned |
| LLM | A model that predicts the next token | Interview questions, answer evaluation | Writing a follow-up question | Called through a provider interface |
| Fine-tuning | Further training on a task | Two QLoRA pipelines | Teaching a strict JSON format | Adapters only; base frozen |
| SFT | Fine-tuning on input–target pairs | Both pipelines | Resume → expected JSON | Completion-only loss |
| PEFT | Training few parameters | LoRA adapters | Sticky notes on a textbook | About 1% trainable |
| LoRA | Low-rank adapters added to weight matrices | r 16, α 32 on 7 projections | Two thin matrices instead of one big one | `W + (α/r)·B·A` |
| QLoRA | LoRA with a 4-bit base model | Fits a T4 | Smaller print, same notes | NF4 quantization via bitsandbytes |
| Quantization | Fewer bits per weight | 4-bit loading | Rounding to fewer decimal places | Trades a little precision for memory |
| Transformer | The architecture behind LLMs | Qwen3 models | Words looking at each other | Attention plus feed-forward layers |
| Attention | Weighting which tokens matter to each token | Inside the models | "it" attending to its noun | Query–key–value projections; LoRA attaches here |
| Tokenization | Splitting text into model units | Length limits of 3,072 and 4,096 tokens | "unhappiness" → pieces | Limits are in tokens, not words |
| Inference | Running a trained model | One call with a timeout | Asking a question | Validation and fallback follow |
| Hallucination | Fluent output without basis | Guarded by schemas, grounding, IDs | A made-up URL | Reduced and counted, not eliminated |
| Prompt injection | Instructions hidden in input data | Structural limits only | "Ignore the rubric" inside a resume | No dedicated filter; scores are code-computed |

## Recommendation, similarity and metrics

| Concept | Definition | In CareerPilot | Simple example | Technical point |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Recommendation system | Suggesting relevant items | Resource ranking; skill recommender (not live) | "Learn Docker next" | Deterministic scoring; item-based CF |
| Ranking | Ordering items by a score | Resources, mentors, gaps | Best resource first | Additive scores with reproducible tie-breaks |
| Cosine similarity | Angle between vectors | Job match, RAG | Same direction = similar | Equals the dot product for unit vectors |
| TF-IDF | Term frequency × inverse document frequency | **Not used** | — | The project uses hashed TF without IDF |
| Accuracy | Share of correct predictions | Classifier: 0.735 (synthetic) | 73 of 100 right | Misleading with imbalanced classes |
| Precision | Correct among predicted positives | Per-class in the classifier | Of flagged, how many were right | TP / (TP + FP) |
| Recall | Found among actual positives | Per-class; Recall@K for the recommender | Of real ones, how many found | TP / (TP + FN) |
| F1 | Harmonic mean of precision and recall | Macro F1 0.737 | One balanced number | 2PR / (P + R) |
| Overfitting | Memorising training data | Guarded by validation loss and early stopping | Good on practice, bad on the exam | Training loss falls, validation loss rises |
| Underfitting | Not learning enough | Career model v1 | Stopped studying too early | 37 updates; loss still falling |
| Train / validation / test split | Separate data for learning, tuning and final check | Split by cluster or learner profile | Practice, mock, final exam | Prevents leakage; test used once |

# Technical glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Adapter | The small set of trained LoRA weights saved after fine-tuning |
| Agent | A class with one responsibility and typed input and output |
| Alias | An alternative spelling mapped to a canonical skill name |
| APIE | Adaptive Placement Intelligence Engine; computes the readiness score |
| Append-only | Records are added, never changed, to keep history |
| ATS | Applicant Tracking System; software that screens resumes |
| Audit log | A record of sensitive actions and who performed them |
| Band | A readiness category: At Risk, Needs Improvement, Placement Ready, Highly Ready |
| Base model | The pre-trained model before fine-tuning |
| bcrypt | A slow, salted password-hashing function |
| bitsandbytes | The library that loads models in 4-bit or 8-bit |
| Bootstrap sample | A random sample with replacement, used by Random Forest |
| Canonical skill | The single official name for a skill and its aliases |
| Capability (Linux) | A fine-grained root privilege; all are dropped in the sandbox |
| cgroup | A Linux feature that limits a process's CPU, memory and process count |
| Checkpoint | A saved state during training |
| Chunking | Splitting a document into overlapping pieces for retrieval |
| Code splitting | Loading page code only when the page is opened |
| Collaborative filtering | Recommending items that co-occur with what a user has |
| Comparator | The judge component that compares returned and expected values |

| CORS | Browser rule controlling which origins may call an API |

| Early stopping | Ending training when validation loss stops improving |
| Embedding | A numeric vector representing text |
| Epoch | One pass over the training data |
| ESCO | The European skills and occupations classification |
| Evidence coverage | The share of readiness components that have data |

| FAISS | A library for fast vector search |
| FastAPI | The Python web framework used by the AI service |
| Feature hashing | Mapping tokens to vector positions with a hash function |
| Feature importance | How much a feature contributes to a tree model's splits |
| Fork bomb | A program that creates processes endlessly |
| Gradient accumulation | Summing gradients over small batches before an update |
| Gradient checkpointing | Saving memory by recomputing activations in the backward pass |

| Helmet | Express middleware that sets security headers |

| JD | Job description |

| LoRA | Low-Rank Adaptation |

| MAE | Mean Absolute Error |

| Monaco | The code editor component from VS Code |

| O*NET | The US occupational information database |
